title: Probabilistic deep learning
text:
These notes gather the probabilistic concepts that underlie most of modern machine learning: information theory (entropy, cross-entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence), maximum likelihood estimation, the probabilistic interpretation of supervised and unsupervised learning, Bayesian estimation and variational inference.
The common thread is that virtually every learning algorithm fits a parameterized distribution p_\theta(x) to data sampled from an unknown distribution p(x), which amounts to minimizing the KL divergence between the two.

title: Information theory
text:
Entropy
Information theory was born from a very practical question. In the 1920s, engineers at Bell Labs wanted to know how fast messages could be sent over telegraph and telephone lines (Hartley, 1928; Nyquist, 1924). In 1948, Claude Shannon gave a complete answer, in a paper that founded the field (Shannon, 1948): information can be measured, in bits, and this measure tells exactly how much a message can be compressed and how fast it can be transmitted through a noisy channel.
Shannon’s key idea is that the information carried by a message has nothing to do with its meaning, only with how surprising it is. A message that you could have predicted tells you nothing new. Think of the morning news:
This is also why messages can be compressed. In an English text, the letter following a “q” is almost always a “u”: transmitting it is a waste, as the receiver could have guessed it. Only the unpredictable parts of a message really need to be transmitted, and the more predictable a source is, the more its messages can be compressed.
Why should machine learning care about telephone lines? Because predicting and compressing are two sides of the same coin. A model that predicts the data well assigns them a high probability: it is not surprised by them, and could therefore encode them with few bits. The cross-entropy loss used to train classifiers and language models (Cross-entropy) is exactly the average number of bits (or nats) that the model needs to encode the data: training a language model to predict the next word is training it to compress text. The quantities introduced in this chapter, entropy, cross-entropy and the Kullback-Leibler divergence, will be used throughout this book to measure how well a model fits the data.
Formally, the key concept of information theory is the entropy of a random variable X, whose outcomes x follow the probability distribution p(x) = P(X = x): a probability mass function (pmf) for discrete variables, a probability density function (pdf) for continuous ones. The entropy measures how much information is contained, on average, in the outcomes of X. It is built on the information carried by each single outcome.
A useful measurement of how surprising an outcome x of a random variable X with pdf/pmf p(x) is, is the self-information:
I(x) = - \log P(X = x) = - \log p(x)
When P(X = x) is 1, the self-information is 0, as the result is certain and deterministic: it brings no information. When P(X = x) is close to 0, the self-information is very high, as it is very surprising that x happens.
Depending on which log is used, the self-information has different units, but it is just a rescaling: the base never matters as we are going to compare it to other values.
The entropy (or Shannon entropy) of a random variable X is the expected value of the self-information of its outcomes:
H(X) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [I(x)] = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [- \log p(x)]
The entropy only depends on the distribution p(x) of the random variable, not on the values of its outcomes, so it is also written H(p), the notation we use when comparing two distributions (Cross-entropy).
It measures the uncertainty, randomness or information content of the random variable.
In the discrete case, the expectation is defined as a sum over the outcomes, weighted by the probability that they happen:
H(X) = - \sum_x P(X=x) \, \log P(X=x)
In the continuous case, we need to use an integral to get the differential entropy (or continuous entropy):
H(X) = - \int_x p(x) \, \log p(x) \, dx
The entropy of a Bernoulli variable is maximal when both outcomes are equiprobable. If a variable is deterministic (probability is either 0 or 1), its entropy is minimal and equal to zero.
The entropy has equivalent properties to probabilities, where products are replaced by additions and divisions are replaced by subtractions:
H(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim X, y \sim Y} [- \log P(X=x, Y=y)]
H(X | Y) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim X, y \sim Y} [- \log p(x | y)]  = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim X, y \sim Y} [- \log \frac{p(x , y)}{p(y)}]
which gives, as \log turns divisions into subtractions:
H(X | Y) = H(X, Y) - H(Y)
H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y)
H(X | Y) = H(X)
H(Y |X) = H(X |Y) + H(Y) - H(X)

“The sun rose this morning” is almost certain: it happens every day, and announcing it carries almost no information. It is not newsworthy.
“The sun did not rise this morning” would be extremely surprising, as it is almost impossible: it would carry a lot of information, and definitely make the news.

NoteDifferential entropy is not quite an entropy





The differential entropy is not an exact equivalent of the discrete entropy:

It can be negative: a density can be larger than 1, so - \log p(x) can be negative. For example, the differential entropy of a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) is \frac{1}{2} \log (2 \pi e \sigma^2), which is negative for small values of \sigma.
It depends on the units of x: measuring x in millimeters instead of meters multiplies the density by 10^{-3}, and adds \log 1000 to the differential entropy.
It is not the limit of the discrete entropy when the continuous variable is discretized more and more finely: with bins of width \Delta, the discrete entropy is approximately H(X) - \log \Delta, which diverges when \Delta \rightarrow 0, as describing a real number exactly would require an infinite number of bits.

These problems disappear in the KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence), which compares two distributions: as a difference between a cross-entropy and an entropy, the problematic terms cancel out. The KL divergence between two continuous distributions is always positive or zero, and does not depend on the units, which is one reason why machine learning relies on it. title: Information theory
text:
Mutual information
The most important information measurement between two variables is the mutual information MI (or information gain):

    I(X, Y) = H(X) - H(X | Y) = H(Y) - H(Y | X)

It measures how much information the variable Y holds on X (and reciprocally):

If the two variables are independent, the MI is 0: X is as uncertain, whether you know Y or not.


    I (X, Y) = 0


If the two variables are dependent, knowing Y gives you information on X, which becomes less random, i.e. less uncertain / surprising or more predictable.


    I (X, Y) > 0

If you can fully predict X when you know Y, it becomes deterministic (H(X|Y)=0) so the mutual information is maximal (I(X, Y) = H(X)).

title: Information theory
text:
Cross-entropy
The entropy, joint entropy and mutual information are properties of random variables. The cross-entropy and the KL divergence compare two probability distributions p and q defined over the same outcomes x. The cross-entropy between p and q is defined as:

    H(p, q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log q(x)]

It measures the entropy of the outcomes of p for the distribution q, i.e. how surprising samples of p are for q. If p and q are the same, the cross-entropy is the same as the entropy of p. If they are different, the samples of p become surprising for q, i.e. they have a low likelihood q(x).






Figure 2.3: The cross-entropy measures the overlap between two probability distributions: it is the average of - \log q(x_i) over samples x_i of p, which is high when these samples are unlikely under q (short orange segments).



The cross-entropy is the mathematical expectation of the negative log-likelihood that a sample x taken from the distribution p could also come from the distribution q. It measures how many bits of information one would need to distinguish the two distributions p and q.

If the two distributions are the same almost everywhere, one cannot distinguish samples from the two distributions. The cross-entropy is the same as the entropy of p.
If the two distributions are different, one can tell whether a sample x comes from p or q, as it will be unlikely under one of them. The cross-entropy would then be higher than the entropy of p.

In layman’s terms, the cross-entropy measures the overlap (or distance) between the two distributions: when the distributions are the same, the cross-entropy is minimal; when they are different, it is high.

title: Information theory
text:
Kullback-Leibler divergence
In practice, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence \text{KL}(p || q) is a better measurement of the similarity (statistical distance) between two probability distributions:

    \text{KL}(p || q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}]

The KL divergence is linked to the cross-entropy by:

    \text{KL}(p || q) = H(p, q) - H(p)

as:

    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}] = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log q(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log p(x)]

If the two distributions are the same almost everywhere, the KL divergence is zero. If the two distributions are different, the KL divergence is positive. Minimizing the KL between two distributions is therefore the same as making the two distributions “equal” or similar.
However, the KL is not a metric (a distance), as it is not symmetric:

    \text{KL}(p || q) \neq \text{KL}(q || p)

The two directions behave very differently when they are minimized, as we will see in Forward vs. reverse KL. Other divergences are symmetric. The Jensen-Shannon divergence compares both distributions to their average m = \frac{1}{2} (p + q):

    \text{JS}(p, q) = \dfrac{1}{2} \, \text{KL}(p || m) + \dfrac{1}{2} \, \text{KL}(q || m)

It is symmetric, \text{JS}(p, q) = \text{JS}(q, p), and always finite, even when q(x) = 0 where p(x) > 0, as the average m is positive wherever one of the two distributions is. It is zero when the distributions are equal, and at most \log 2, a value reached when they do not overlap at all.
Refer to https://towardsdatascience.com/entropy-cross-entropy-and-kl-divergence-explained-b09cdae917a for nice visual explanations of the cross-entropy and KL divergence.

title: Maximum likelihood estimation
text:
MLE for the univariate normal distribution
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a statistical method to estimate the parameters \theta of a parametric family of probability distributions p(x; \theta) = p_\theta(x) that best explains some observed data samples X = \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N coming from an unknown distribution p(x).
The N samples x_i come from some unknown probability distribution \mathcal{D}. An important assumption is that the samples are i.i.d (independent and identically distributed), i.e. that they all come from the same distribution and are not correlated with each other (the value of one sample does not influence the value taken by the next one).
We then assume a particular parametric family of probability distributions, with a probability density function (pdf) p_\theta(x). For example, the pdf of the family of normal distributions is:
p(x ; \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \, \exp{- \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \, \sigma^2}}
where \mu is the mean of the distribution and \sigma its standard deviation. The family of normal distributions is parameterized by \mu and \sigma.
The problem is to find the values of \mu and \sigma which best explain the observations \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N. Said otherwise: among all possible normal distributions with different values for \mu and \sigma, which one is the most likely origin of the samples \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N? In Figure 3.1, the orange normal distribution fits the data better than the green one. But how do we find its parameters?
The idea of MLE is to maximize the joint density function for all observations p_\theta(X), i.e. the joint probability of observing the N samples x_i given the current value of the parameters \theta. This function is also called the likelihood function L(\theta; X) (or simply L(\theta)), i.e. the likelihood that the parameters \theta explain the data X:
L(\theta)  = p_\theta( X) = p_\theta( x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N)
Note that p_\theta( X ) is a joint probability, but L(\theta) is a likelihood: the first is asking about the data, while the second is asking about the parameters.
When the samples are i.i.d, the joint probability of observing the N samples x_i is equal to the product of their individual probabilities, as P(X, Y) = P(X) \, P(Y) when X and Y are independent:
L(\theta) = p_\theta( X ) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p_\theta(x_i )
Intuitively, this means that when the pdf of the distribution p_\theta(x_i) is high for all samples, the samples likely come from that distribution as the likelihood will be high.
This means that if we know the pdf of the family of distributions, we can compute the likelihood function and find its mode, i.e. the value of \theta for which the likelihood is maximal:
\theta_\text{MLE} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, L(\theta)
For mathematical convenience, we can also maximize the log-likelihood function:
l(\theta) = \log L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(x_i )
as the log function is monotonically increasing on \Re^+ and the likelihood function is positive (product of probabilities).
\theta_\text{MLE} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, l(\theta) = \text{argmax}_\theta \, \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(x_i )
In machine learning, it is customary to minimize the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which is exactly the same thing:
\theta_\text{MLE} = \text{argmin}_\theta \, \text{NLL}(\theta) = \text{argmin}_\theta \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p_\theta(x_i )
Any optimization method can be used, either analytic optimization if we have the analytical form of the pdf, or approximate optimization methods such as gradient descent.
Note that the probability distribution p(x; \theta_\text{MLE}) with the best parameters is not equal to the true distribution of the data \mathcal{D}: it is only the best approximation we can get using 1) that particular family of distributions (the pdf of \mathcal{D} might not have the Gaussian shape of the normal distribution) and 2) those samples (the more samples, the better).
For the normal distribution, the likelihood function is:
\begin{aligned}
L(\mu, \sigma) & = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p(x_i ; \mu, \sigma ) \\
& = \prod_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \, \exp{- \frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\\
& = (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}})^N \, \prod_{i=1}^{N} \exp{- \frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\\
& = (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}})^N \, \exp{- \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\\
\end{aligned}
To find the mode of L(\mu, \sigma), we would need to search where its gradient is equal to zero:
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial L(\mu, \sigma)}{\partial \mu} = 0 \\
\dfrac{\partial L(\mu, \sigma)}{\partial \sigma} = 0 \\
\end{cases}
The likelihood function is complex to differentiate because of all the products involved, so we consider instead the log-likelihood function:
\begin{aligned}
l(\mu, \sigma) & = \log L(\mu, \sigma) \\
& = \log \left((\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}})^N \, \exp{- \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} \right)\\
& = - \frac{N}{2} \log (2\pi \sigma^2) - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\\
\end{aligned}
The advantage of using the log function is that it turns products into sums, and exponentials into linear terms, which is much more differentiation-friendly.
The maximum of the log-likelihood function respects:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial l(\mu, \sigma)}{\partial \mu} & = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)}{\sigma^2} = 0 \\
\frac{\partial l(\mu, \sigma)}{\partial \sigma} & = - \frac{N}{2} \frac{4 \pi \sigma}{2 \pi \sigma^2} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{\sigma^3} \\
& = - \frac{N}{\sigma} + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{\sigma^3} = 0\\
\end{aligned}
By solving these two equations, we obtain:
\mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \qquad\qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2
Unsurprisingly, the mean and variance of the normal distribution which best explains the data are the empirical mean and variance of the data…
The same principle can be applied to estimate the parameters of any distribution based on samples: normal, exponential, Bernoulli, Poisson, etc.
Maximum likelihood estimation is a good method when 1) the number of samples is big enough (central limit theorem, see Bayesian estimation) and 2) we do not care about the uncertainty of our estimator.

title: Bayesian estimation
text:
Central limit theorem: frequentist estimation
Suppose we have an unknown distribution X (it does not have to be normal) with expected value \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] and variance \sigma^2. We can take randomly N samples from X to compute the sample average:
S_N = \frac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N x_i
The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that:
S_N \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}})
If we perform the sampling multiple times, even with a few samples, the average of the sampling averages will be very close to the expected value. The more samples we get, the smaller the variance of the estimates. Although the distribution X can be anything, the sampling averages are normally distributed.
MLE (Maximum likelihood estimation) is a frequentist estimation method as it only relies on the obtained samples, not on additional knowledge one might have about the underlying distribution. In Bayesian statistics (Bayes, 1763), this additional knowledge takes the form of a prior distribution p(\theta) over the parameters \theta of the model.

title: Bayesian estimation
text:
Maximum a posteriori (MAP)

Bayes’ rule on the parameters
In MLE, the parameters \theta are fixed but unknown quantities: we search for the value that maximizes the likelihood p(X | \theta) = p_\theta(X) of the data, and that’s it. In Bayesian statistics, the parameters are themselves random variables. Before seeing any data, our belief about their value is described by the prior distribution p(\theta). After observing the data X = \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N, this belief is updated into the posterior distribution p(\theta | X) using Bayes’ rule:

    p(\theta | X) = \dfrac{p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta)}{p(X)}

The posterior depends on:

the likelihood p(X | \theta): how well the parameters \theta explain the data, exactly as in MLE.
the prior p(\theta): which values of the parameters are plausible before seeing the data.
the evidence p(X): the probability of the data under all possible values of the parameters.

The evidence is obtained by marginalizing over the parameters:

    p(X) = \int_\theta p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta) \, d\theta

It does not depend on \theta anymore: it is only a normalization constant ensuring that the posterior integrates to one.
The idea of maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation is to search for the value of the parameters that is the most probable after having observed the data, i.e. the mode of the posterior distribution:

    \theta_\text{MAP} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, p(\theta | X) = \text{argmax}_\theta \, \dfrac{p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta)}{p(X)}

As the evidence does not depend on \theta, we do not need to compute it to find the mode of the posterior. This is lucky, as the integral over all possible parameters is generally intractable:

    \theta_\text{MAP} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta)

For the same reasons as in MLE, we rather maximize the logarithm of this quantity. When the samples are i.i.d, the likelihood is a product over the samples, so the log-posterior (up to a constant) is a sum:

    \theta_\text{MAP} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, \log p(X | \theta) + \log p(\theta) = \text{argmax}_\theta \, \sum_{i=1}^N \log p(x_i | \theta) + \log p(\theta)

or, if you prefer minimizing the negative log-likelihood:

    \theta_\text{MAP} = \text{argmin}_\theta \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p(x_i | \theta) - \log p(\theta)

The MAP objective is the MLE objective plus an additional term, the log-prior, which pulls the estimate towards the values of the parameters that we believe are plausible.
If the prior is uniform (all values of \theta are equally plausible), \log p(\theta) is a constant and MAP reduces to MLE:

    p(\theta) = \text{cst} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_\text{MAP} = \theta_\text{MLE}

MLE is therefore a special case of MAP where we have no prior knowledge about the parameters.


MAP for the mean of a normal distribution
Let’s go back to the example of the univariate normal distribution from Maximum likelihood estimation. To keep the math simple, we suppose that the standard deviation \sigma of the data is known and only estimate its mean \mu. The likelihood of the N samples is:

    p(X | \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \, \exp{- \frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}

Before seeing the data, we believe that the mean should be around a value \mu_0, with an uncertainty \sigma_0. This translates into a normal prior on the parameter \mu:

    p(\mu) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \sigma_0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma_0^2}} \, \exp{- \frac{(\mu - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}}

The log-posterior is, up to constant terms that do not depend on \mu:

    \log p(\mu | X) = - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{(\mu - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} + \text{cst}

Its maximum is reached when its derivative w.r.t \mu is zero:

    \frac{\partial \log p(\mu | X)}{\partial \mu} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\mu - \mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} = 0

which gives:

    \mu \, (\frac{N}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2}

By introducing the empirical mean of the data \bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i, i.e. the MLE estimate, we obtain:

    \mu_\text{MAP} = \dfrac{N \, \sigma_0^2}{N \, \sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2} \, \bar{x} + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{N \, \sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2} \, \mu_0

The MAP estimate is a weighted average between the MLE estimate \bar{x} and the prior mean \mu_0. The two weights sum to one, and their relative importance depends on the number of samples and on how confident we are in the prior:

When there are few samples (N \rightarrow 0), the estimate stays close to the prior \mu_0: we do not have enough evidence to change our mind.
When there are many samples (N \rightarrow \infty), the weight of the prior vanishes and the MAP estimate tends to the MLE estimate \bar{x}: the data overrides the prior.
When the prior is very uncertain (\sigma_0 \rightarrow \infty), the prior becomes uniform and we also recover MLE.
When the prior is very certain (\sigma_0 \rightarrow 0), the estimate sticks to \mu_0, whatever the data says.

Figure 4.2 illustrates this with a prior \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and data sampled from \mathcal{N}(3, 2). With a single sample, the posterior stays close to the prior. As more samples are observed, the likelihood becomes sharper and pulls the posterior towards the empirical mean \bar{x}, while the prior loses its influence.






Figure 4.2: Prior, (normalized) likelihood and posterior of the mean \mu for N = 1, 5 and 50 samples drawn from \mathcal{N}(3, 2), with a prior \mathcal{N}(0, 1). The thin vertical lines show the MLE estimate \bar{x} (orange) and the MAP estimate \mu_\text{MAP} (green); the dotted gray line is the true mean.



In this particular case, the posterior is itself a normal distribution (the normal prior is said to be conjugate to the normal likelihood), whose mean is \mu_\text{MAP} and whose variance \sigma_N^2 is given by:

    \frac{1}{\sigma_N^2} = \frac{N}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_0^2}

The more samples we observe, the smaller the variance of the posterior: our uncertainty about the parameter decreases with the amount of data, as for the sampling averages in the central limit theorem.


MAP and regularization
MAP estimation has a direct interpretation in machine learning. Let’s consider a neural network with parameters \theta trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the data, for example the cross-entropy loss of a classifier (Softmax classifier for discrete distributions). If we put a normal prior with zero mean on each parameter \theta_j:

    p(\theta) = \prod_j \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma_0^2}} \, \exp{- \frac{\theta_j^2}{2\sigma_0^2}}

the negative log-prior becomes:

    - \log p(\theta) = \frac{1}{2 \sigma_0^2} \, \sum_j \theta_j^2 + \text{cst} = \frac{1}{2 \sigma_0^2} \, ||\theta||^2 + \text{cst}

The MAP objective is then the usual loss function plus a penalty on the squared norm of the parameters:

    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p_\theta(x_i) + \lambda \, ||\theta||^2 \qquad \text{with} \qquad \lambda = \frac{1}{2 \sigma_0^2}

This is exactly L2 regularization (or weight decay)! Adding weight decay to the loss function is the same as assuming that the parameters are normally distributed around zero, and the regularization coefficient \lambda controls the width of this prior: a strong regularization means a narrow prior, i.e. a strong belief that the parameters should stay small.
Similarly, a Laplace prior p(\theta_j) \propto \exp{- \frac{|\theta_j|}{b}} leads to L1 regularization (the lasso), which favors sparse parameters.


Limitations of MAP
MAP is still a point estimate: it returns a single value of the parameters, the mode of the posterior, and discards the rest of the distribution. It therefore does not tell us how uncertain the estimate is. In the normal example above, we could get the variance of the posterior analytically, but this is rarely the case.
Full Bayesian inference keeps the whole posterior distribution p(\theta | X), and makes predictions by averaging over all possible values of the parameters, weighted by their posterior probability:

    p(x | X) = \int_\theta p(x | \theta) \, p(\theta | X) \, d\theta

This requires computing the evidence p(X) to normalize the posterior, which is precisely the intractable integral that MAP avoids. Approximating such intractable posteriors with a tractable parameterized distribution is the main idea of variational inference (Variational inference).

title: Learning paradigms
text:
Discriminative learning (supervised learning, classification, regression)
We can think of three main paradigms in machine learning.
In discriminative learning, we try to model a conditional probability mapping a probability distribution X into a probability distribution Y:
x \sim X, y\sim Y: p(y | x)
We create a neural network p_\theta(y | x) whose goal is to approximate the data distribution by taking an input x and returning a parameterization of the distribution of y.

    x(("<i>x</i>"))
    f["<i>f</i><sub>θ</sub>"]
    y(("<i>p</i><sub>θ</sub>(<i>y</i> | <i>x</i>)"))
If Y is a discrete (categorical) distribution, we are doing a classification. We just need to model Y using a Gibbs / Boltzmann distribution (i.e. a softmax layer) and we are good.
If Y is continuous and Gaussian, but we only care about its expectation (\mathbb{E}[Y|X]), we are performing regression. If we also want its variance, it is Bayesian regression.
If Y is continuous and we want its distribution (of an unknown family) for uncertainty estimation, we need to use mixtures of Gaussians like in Mixture Density Networks (MDN, see Mixture density networks for continuous distributions).

title: Learning paradigms
text:
Generative modeling (unsupervised learning)
In unsupervised learning, we only get samples x of an unknown distribution X:

    x \sim X: p(x)

In density estimation, we want to train a neural network to predict the likelihood of a sample x.





flowchart LR
    x --> f --> y
    x(("<i>x</i>"))
    f["<i>f</i><sub>θ</sub>"]
    y(("<i>p</i><sub>θ</sub>(<i>x</i>)"))






This is vanilla maximum likelihood estimation (MLE, Maximum likelihood estimation). This can be useful for anomaly detection: if the predicted likelihood of a new sample is below a threshold, it might be an anomaly.
Generative modeling is quite different. We want to generate a new sample from the data distribution (e.g. generate new images of cats). In most methods we want to learn a mapping between a simple known distribution (typically the standard normal distribution) and the data distribution. A sample z from the “latent” prior distribution should be transformed into a sample x of the (approximated) data distribution.





flowchart LR
    x --> f --> y
    x(("<i>z</i> ~ 𝒩(0, 1)"))
    f["<i>f</i><sub>θ</sub>"]
    y(("<i>x</i> ~ <i>p</i><sub>θ</sub>(<i>x</i>)"))






This is what the decoder of a VAE (variational inference, Variational inference), the generator of a GAN, or a diffusion model does.

title: Learning paradigms
text:
Autoregressive modeling (self-supervised learning)
Finally, autoregressive models predict part of the sample based on the rest. For temporal sequences, it is often next item prediction:

    p(x_{t+1} | x_t, x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_0)

Transformers for language modeling learn the categorical probability distribution of the next token (classification over thousands of vocabulary tokens) given the history (aka prompt).





flowchart LR
    x --> f --> y
    x(("<i>x</i><sub>0</sub>, …, <i>x</i><sub>t-1</sub>, <i>x</i><sub>t</sub>"))
    f["LLM"]
    y(("<i>x</i><sub>t+1</sub>"))






There also exist autoregressive vision models, where the next pixel is predicted depending on the others (PixelCNN).
Masked learning (predict part of the sample given the rest) somehow fits in this category.

title: Learning paradigms
text:
Summary
In virtually all machine learning paradigms, we learn a parameterized probability distribution p_\theta(x) (whatever the meaning of x) and want to make it close to the data distribution p(x).
The only way to do that is to minimize the KL divergence between the two distributions:

    \theta^* = \text{argmin}_\theta \; \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x))

However, we generally do not know the explicit form of p(x): we only have access to samples x_i from which we need to approximate the KL.

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning
text:
Closed form of the KL divergence for normal distributions
Let us now look at maximum likelihood estimation / KL minimization from the information theory point of view.
The definition of the KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence) relies on the mathematical expectation of the negative log-likelihood of the outcomes of p:
\text{KL}(p || q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}]
There are basically two ways to compute the KL, one relying on closed analytical forms, the other on sampling. We focus here on the first one; sampling methods are the topic of Monte Carlo and importance sampling.
The first method is possible when both distributions are normal distributions. Let us suppose that p and q are both univariate normal distributions:
p(x) = \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_p, \sigma_p) \qquad\qquad\qquad q(x) = \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_q, \sigma_q)
We can use the known pdf of normal distributions to get the KL:
\begin{aligned}
\text{KL}(p || q) &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{\mathcal{N}(x; \mu_q, \sigma_q)}{\mathcal{N}(x; \mu_p, \sigma_p)}] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[ \log \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_p, \sigma_p) - \log \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_q, \sigma_q)] \\
\end{aligned}
As:
\mathcal{N}(x ; \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \, \exp{- \dfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \, \sigma^2}}
the log-likelihood of a normal distribution is:
\begin{aligned}
\log \mathcal{N}(x ; \mu, \sigma) &= \log [\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \, \exp{- \dfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \, \sigma^2}}] \\
&= -\dfrac{1}{2} \log 2 \pi \sigma^2 - \dfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \, \sigma^2}\\
&= - \dfrac{1}{2} [ \log 2 \pi + 2 \, \log \sigma + \dfrac{(x - \mu)^2}{\sigma^2} ]\\
\end{aligned}
This gives for the KL:
\begin{aligned}
\text{KL}(p || q) &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[ \log \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_p, \sigma_p) - \log \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_q, \sigma_q)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[\dfrac{1}{2} \, [2 \, \log \sigma_q + \dfrac{(x - \mu_q)^2}{\sigma_q^2} - 2 \, \log \sigma_p - \dfrac{(x - \mu_p)^2}{\sigma_p^2}]]\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [\log \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} + \dfrac{(x - \mu_q)^2}{2 \sigma_q^2} - \dfrac{(x - \mu_p)^2}{2 \sigma_p^2}]\\
&= \log \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} + \dfrac{1}{2 \sigma_q^2} \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_q)^2] - \dfrac{1}{2 \sigma_p^2} \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p)^2]\\
\end{aligned}
By definition of the variance, we have:
\sigma_p^2 = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p)^2]
Moreover, as \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [x - \mu_p] = 0:
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_q)^2] &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p + \mu_p - \mu_q)^2]\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p)^2] + 2 \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p) \, (\mu_p - \mu_q)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(\mu_p - \mu_q)^2] \\
&= \sigma_p^2 + (\mu_p - \mu_q)^2 \\
\end{aligned}
which gives:
\begin{aligned}
\text{KL}(p || q) &= \log \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} + \dfrac{1}{2 \sigma_q^2} \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_q)^2] - \dfrac{1}{2 \sigma_p^2} \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(x - \mu_p)^2]\\
&= \log \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} + \dfrac{\sigma_p^2 + (\mu_p - \mu_q)^2}{2 \sigma_q^2} - \dfrac{\sigma_p^2}{2 \sigma_p^2} \\
\end{aligned}
We can check that when \mu_p = \mu_q and \sigma_p = \sigma_q, the KL is zero.
When q is the standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1), we have:
\text{KL}(p || \mathcal{N}(0, 1)) = \dfrac{1}{2} [\sigma_p^2 + \mu_p^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_p^2]

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning
text:
Equivalence between KL and cross-entropy
Let’s now consider that the samples X = \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N come from some unknown distribution p (the data), while Y comes from a parameterized family of probability distributions p_\theta(x) with parameters \theta (the model). The KL divergence is expressed as:

\begin{aligned}
\text{KL}(p || p_\theta) & = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{p_\theta(x)}{p(x)}] \\
& = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log p_\theta(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log p(x)] \\
& = H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) - H(p(x)) \\
\end{aligned}

The KL between the data and the model is the difference between their cross-entropy and the entropy of the data.
If we want the model p_\theta to explain the data \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N sampled from p, we want the KL divergence between p_\theta and p to be zero, as both distributions would then be the same. In other terms, we search for a value of \theta where the KL divergence between the model and the data is minimal: the KL is always positive, so its minimum is 0.

    \theta^* = \text{argmin}_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x))

Minimizing the KL with respect to \theta requires access to its gradient, i.e. the partial derivatives of the KL divergence with respect to each parameter. Gradient descent can for example be used to iteratively update the parameters in the opposite direction to this gradient:

    \Delta \theta = - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x))

Let us have a look at this gradient:

    \nabla_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x)) = \nabla_\theta \, H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) - \nabla_\theta \, H(p(x))

The gradient of the KL is the gradient of the cross-entropy minus the gradient of the entropy of the data. However, the data distribution p(x) does not depend on the parameters \theta of the model, so the gradient of the entropy of the data is zero:

    \nabla_\theta \, H(p(x)) = 0

This means that the gradient of the KL is the same as the gradient of the cross-entropy:

    \nabla_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x)) = \nabla_\theta \, H(p(x), p_\theta(x))

Minimizing the KL divergence between a model and the data is the same as minimizing their cross-entropy!
The KL divergence and the cross-entropy only differ by a constant term, the entropy of the data, which does not depend on the model. The value of \theta that minimizes one also minimizes the other.
Let us now estimate the cross-entropy:

    H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log p_\theta(x)]

Using N samples \{x_i\}_{i=1}^N from the data, we can approximate this expectation with a Monte Carlo estimate (Monte Carlo and importance sampling), i.e. the average of - \log p_\theta(x) over the samples:

    H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p_\theta(x_i) = - \dfrac{1}{N} \, l(\theta)

where l(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(x_i) is the log-likelihood of the model on the data that we introduced in maximum likelihood estimation (Maximum likelihood estimation). Maximizing the log-likelihood minimizes the cross-entropy and therefore the KL divergence.
This means that MLE is strictly equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence (or cross-entropy) between the model p_\theta and the distribution of the data p!

    \theta_\text{MLE} = \text{argmax}_\theta \, l(\theta) = \text{argmin}_\theta \, H(p(x), p_\theta(x)) = \text{argmin}_\theta \, \text{KL}(p(x) || p_\theta(x))

Any machine learning model with a probabilistic interpretation that tries to fit a parameterized model to some data is implicitly minimizing the KL divergence between the two distributions.
Depending on the assumption about the underlying distribution, we can use the following neural network architectures:

Discrete / categorical / multinoulli distribution: softmax classifier.
Continuous distribution: mixture density network (MDN, Bishop, 1994) or Gaussian Process regression (GPR, but it is a nonparametric kernel-based probabilistic model, not a neural network).

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning
text:
Forward vs. reverse KL
The KL divergence is not symmetric (Kullback-Leibler divergence): \text{KL}(p || q) and \text{KL}(q || p) are different quantities, and minimizing one or the other leads to very different results. Let’s call p the target distribution and q the approximation we fit to it. Maximum likelihood fits a model q = p_\theta to the distribution of the data p; variational inference (Variational inference) will fit an approximate posterior q = q_\phi(z | x) to a true posterior p = p_\theta(z | x).

Two directions
The forward KL is an expectation under the target:

    \text{KL}(p || q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}]

Estimating it requires samples of the target. This is the situation of the previous section: we have data, i.e. samples of p, and minimizing the forward KL is maximum likelihood estimation.
The reverse KL is an expectation under the approximation:

    \text{KL}(q || p) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q(x)}[- \log \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}]

Estimating it requires samples of the approximation, which we choose easy to sample, and the ability to evaluate the target, at least up to its normalization constant: if p(x) = \tilde{p}(x) / Z, then \log p(x) = \log \tilde{p}(x) - \log Z, and the constant \log Z does not change the minimum. This is the situation of Bayesian inference, where the posterior can be evaluated up to the evidence but not sampled: variational inference minimizes the reverse KL.
In practice, the choice of the direction is therefore usually imposed by what we have: samples of the target, or its unnormalized density.


Where is the penalty?
The two directions do not penalize the same errors:

In the forward KL, the log-ratio is weighted by the target p(x). The penalty is very large where p(x) > 0 but q(x) \approx 0, as - \log q(x) explodes, while regions where p(x) \approx 0 do not count at all. The approximation must put mass everywhere the target has mass, even if this means putting mass where the target has none: the forward KL is mass-covering.
In the reverse KL, the log-ratio is weighted by the approximation q(x). The penalty is very large where q(x) > 0 but p(x) \approx 0, while regions where q(x) \approx 0 do not count at all. The approximation must avoid the regions where the target is small, even if this means ignoring whole parts of the target: the reverse KL is mode-seeking.

Figure 6.1 illustrates the difference by fitting a single normal distribution q(x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) to a bimodal target. With the forward KL, the best normal distribution covers both modes: it is broad, and puts most of its mass in the valley between the modes, where the target has almost none. For a normal approximation, the optimum of the forward KL simply matches the mean and the variance of the target. With the reverse KL, the normal distribution settles on one of the modes and ignores the other: there are two local optima, and which one is found depends on the initialization of the parameters.






Figure 6.1: Fitting a normal distribution q(x) to a bimodal target p(x). Left: the forward KL gives a broad distribution covering both modes. Right: the reverse KL has two local optima, each covering one mode only. The target has the weights and widths of the target of Monte Carlo and importance sampling, with modes further apart.



The behavior of the reverse KL depends on how separated the modes are. If they are close to each other, as in the bimodal target of Monte Carlo and importance sampling, covering both modes with a single broad distribution costs less than ignoring one of them, and the reverse KL also prefers a broad fit; the two directions differ more and more when the modes move apart.


Consequences
These two behaviors have practical consequences throughout this book:

Maximum likelihood (forward KL) produces models that try to cover all the data. When the model is not flexible enough, it spreads probability between the modes of the data, and generates “averaged” samples that do not look like any real one, which is one reason for the blurry samples of variational autoencoders (Variational autoencoders).
Variational inference (reverse KL) produces approximate posteriors that are too confident: they underestimate the uncertainty, and can miss whole modes of the posterior. This is the same failure as a too narrow proposal in importance sampling (Importance sampling) or an MCMC chain stuck in one mode (Using MCMC in practice), and an important limitation for the multimodal posteriors of inverse problems (Inverse problems).

Other divergences interpolate between these two behaviors or are symmetric, for example the Jensen-Shannon divergence, which is at the heart of generative adversarial networks.

title: Softmax classifier for discrete distributions
text:
Classification as density estimation
Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning showed that any model with a probabilistic interpretation, fitted to data by maximum likelihood, minimizes the KL divergence between the data and the model. This chapter applies this idea to the most common case in machine learning: classification, where the quantity to predict is discrete. The resulting model, the softmax classifier, is everywhere in deep learning: it is the output layer of image classifiers, and also of language models, which are classifiers predicting the next token among a vocabulary of tens of thousands of words.
In classification, we want to learn a mapping between input vectors \mathbf{x} and a finite number K of classes. In object recognition, the inputs are the pixels of images, and the classes are the names of the objects they represent. The training data is a set of pairs \{(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{t}_i)\}_{i=1}^N, where the targets \mathbf{t}_i (also called labels or ground truth) indicate the class of each input.
In multi-class classification, the target is usually represented by a one-hot encoded vector: a vector of K zeros, except a one at the position of the correct class. For example, with five classes (cat, dog, ship, house, car), an image of a dog is associated with the target:
\mathbf{t} = [\text{cat}, \text{dog}, \text{ship}, \text{house}, \text{car}] = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]
This vector can be read in a probabilistic way: it is a categorical distribution over the classes (a die with one face per class, Sampling from simple distributions), which puts all its probability on the class “dog”:
p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}) = [p(\text{cat}| \mathbf{x}), p(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x}), p(\text{ship}| \mathbf{x}), p(\text{house}| \mathbf{x}), p(\text{car}| \mathbf{x})] = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]
The targets of the training set are therefore samples of an unknown conditional distribution p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}): the probability of each class, given the input. One-hot vectors are only a special case of this distribution, where the class is certain. The targets could perfectly be “soft”, for example [0.1, 0.7, 0, 0, 0.2] for an ambiguous image, or when several annotators disagree.
Classification thus becomes a density estimation problem, as in Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning: we want a parameterized model p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}) that outputs, for each input, a categorical distribution as close as possible to the one of the data.

title: Softmax classifier for discrete distributions
text:
The softmax function
A neural network F_\theta can easily output a vector of K real numbers for each input. These numbers are called the logits \mathbf{z}:

    \mathbf{z} = F_\theta(\mathbf{x})

The logits can take any real value, so they cannot be used directly as probabilities, which must be positive and sum to one. The softmax function \mathcal{S} transforms them into a categorical distribution \mathbf{y}:

    y_k = \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{z})_k = \dfrac{\exp z_k}{\sum_{l=1}^K \exp z_l}

The exponential makes all elements positive, and the denominator normalizes them so that they sum to one (Figure 7.1). The output \mathbf{y} of the network is the model distribution p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}): its element y_k is the predicted probability of the class k.






Figure 7.1: The softmax function transforms logits into a categorical probability distribution.



A few properties help to understand what the softmax does:

It preserves the ranking of the logits: the class with the highest logit gets the highest probability.
It only depends on the differences between the logits: adding the same constant to all logits does not change the probabilities, as the factor \exp c cancels between the numerator and the denominator. Libraries use this property to compute the softmax in a numerically stable way, by subtracting the largest logit first.
It is a smooth version of the argmax: if one logit is much larger than the others, the softmax puts almost all the probability on this class. Dividing the logits by a temperature T before the softmax controls this behavior: a low temperature (T \rightarrow 0) gives a one-hot vector on the most likely class, a high temperature (T \rightarrow \infty) a uniform distribution.

title: Softmax classifier for discrete distributions
text:
The cross-entropy loss
We now have two categorical distributions for each input: the target \mathbf{t}, representing the data, and the prediction \mathbf{y}, representing the model. As in Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning, we want to minimize the KL divergence between them, which is the same as minimizing their cross-entropy (Cross-entropy), as the entropy of the data does not depend on the parameters:

    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{t}) \sim \mathcal{D}} [H(p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}), p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}))] = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{t}) \sim \mathcal{D}} [- \sum_{k=1}^K t_k \, \log y_k]

The cross-entropy between two categorical distributions is a sum over the classes, which can be written as a dot product: - \mathbf{t} \cdot \log \mathbf{y}. With a one-hot target, all terms of the sum are zero except the one of the correct class. For the image of a dog:

    - \mathbf{t} \cdot \log \mathbf{y} = - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \log \, p_\theta(\text{cat}| \mathbf{x}) \\ \log \, p_\theta(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x}) \\ \log \, p_\theta(\text{ship}| \mathbf{x}) \\ \log \, p_\theta(\text{house}| \mathbf{x})\\ \log \, p_\theta(\text{car}| \mathbf{x}) \\ \end{bmatrix} = - \log \, p_\theta(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x})

The loss of a single example is simply the negative log-likelihood of the correct class under the model: we recover maximum likelihood estimation (Maximum likelihood estimation). Its behavior is easy to interpret:

if the model is confident and right (p_\theta(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x}) \approx 1), the loss is close to zero;
if the model is uncertain (p_\theta(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x}) = 1/K, the uniform distribution), the loss is \log K;
if the model is confident and wrong (p_\theta(\text{dog}| \mathbf{x}) \approx 0), the loss is very large: confident mistakes are heavily penalized.

In practice, the expectation is estimated on the training set, or on a minibatch of it, with a Monte Carlo average (The Monte Carlo estimator):

    \mathcal{L}(\theta) \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N - \mathbf{t}_i \cdot \log \mathbf{y}_i

title: Softmax classifier for discrete distributions
text:
The gradient of the loss
To minimize the loss with gradient descent, we need its gradient with respect to the parameters \theta. By the chain rule, it goes through the logits \mathbf{z} = F_\theta(\mathbf{x}), and the combination of the logarithm in the cross-entropy and of the exponential in the softmax makes the gradient with respect to the logits remarkably simple. For a single example with loss l(\theta) = - \mathbf{t} \cdot \log \mathbf{y}:

    \dfrac{\partial l(\theta)}{\partial \mathbf{z}} = - (\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{y})







NoteProof





When differentiating a softmax probability y_l = \dfrac{\exp z_l}{\sum_m \exp z_m} with respect to a logit z_k, two cases have to be considered:

If l = k, \exp z_k appears both in the numerator and in the denominator. The product rule (f\times g)' = f'\, g + f \, g' gives us:


\begin{aligned}
\dfrac{\partial y_k}{\partial z_k} &= \dfrac{\exp z_k}{\sum_m \exp z_m} + \exp z_k \, \dfrac{- \exp z_k}{(\sum_m \exp z_m)^2} \\
&= \dfrac{\exp z_k \, \sum_m \exp z_m - (\exp z_k)^2}{(\sum_m \exp z_m)^2} \\
&= \dfrac{\exp z_k}{\sum_m \exp z_m} \, (1- \dfrac{\exp z_k}{\sum_m \exp z_m})\\
&= y_k \, (1 - y_k)\\
\end{aligned}

This is similar to the derivative of the logistic function.

If l \neq k, z_k only appears in the denominator, so we only need the chain rule:


\begin{aligned}
\dfrac{\partial y_l}{\partial z_k} &= - \exp z_l \, \dfrac{\exp z_k}{(\sum_m \exp z_m)^2} \\
&= - \dfrac{\exp z_k}{\sum_m \exp z_m} \, \dfrac{\exp z_l}{\sum_m \exp z_m} \\
&= - y_k \, y_l \\
\end{aligned}

This allows us to differentiate the cross-entropy:

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial l(\theta)}{\partial z_k} & = - \sum_l \frac{\partial}{\partial z_k} t_l \log y_l =
- \sum_l t_l \frac{\partial \log y_l}{\partial z_k} = - \sum_l \frac{t_l}{y_l} \frac{\partial y_l}{\partial z_k} \\
& = - \frac{t_k}{y_k} \frac{\partial y_k}{\partial z_k} - \sum_{l \neq k} \frac{t_l}{y_l} \frac{\partial y_l}{\partial z_k}
= - \frac{t_k}{y_k} y_k (1-y_k) - \sum_{l \neq k} \frac{t_l}{y_l} (-y_l \, y_k) \\
& = - t_k + t_k \, y_k + \sum_{l \neq k} t_l \, y_k = - t_k + y_k \sum_{l} t_l \\
& = - (t_k - y_k)
\end{aligned}

as the targets sum to one.



The gradient with respect to the logits is the prediction error: the difference between the target and the predicted distribution. This is the same form as the gradient of the mean square error in linear regression, which makes the softmax classifier as easy to train as a regression model:

the logit of the correct class (t_k = 1) is increased by 1 - y_k, i.e. a lot if the model gives it a low probability, and not at all if the model is already certain;
the logits of the wrong classes (t_k = 0) are decreased by y_k, i.e. in proportion of the probability the model wrongly gives them;
when the prediction matches the target, \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{t}, the gradient is zero.

The gradient with respect to the parameters is then obtained by backpropagating this error through the network:

    \nabla_\theta \, \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{t}) \sim \mathcal{D}} [ - (\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{y} ) \times \nabla_\theta \, F_\theta(\mathbf{x})]

The network F_\theta can be anything differentiable: whatever its architecture, training it with the cross-entropy loss minimizes the KL divergence between the categorical distribution of the data and the one of the model.

title: Softmax classifier for discrete distributions
text:
Using the predicted distribution
Once trained, the classifier outputs a full probability distribution over the classes, which can be used in two ways:

For decisions, we usually keep the most probable class, the argmax of \mathbf{y}, as the prediction of the classifier.
For generation, we can sample a class from the categorical distribution \mathbf{y} (Sampling from simple distributions). This is how language models generate text: at each step, the next token is sampled from the softmax output, and the temperature of the softmax controls the trade-off between the most likely continuations (T \rightarrow 0, close to the argmax) and more diverse ones (larger T).

The predicted probabilities also quantify the confidence of the model, but only to a certain extent: a classifier trained with the cross-entropy loss can be confidently wrong on inputs that are very different from its training data. The softmax only represents the uncertainty that is present in the data themselves (ambiguous inputs), not the uncertainty of the model about its own parameters.

title: Mixture density networks for continuous distributions
text:
Mean-variance estimation (MVE)
See https://medium.com/towards-data-science/predicting-the-unpredictable-905f634acc20 for an explanation with code.
The easiest case is when we can assume that the data comes from a normal distribution. All we need to predict is then the mean and the variance of the distribution. This is logically called mean-variance estimation (MVE, Nix and Weigend, 1994).
As for the softmax classifier, the training data is a set of tuples \{\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{t}_i\}_{i=1}^N sampled from the conditional probability distribution p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}), but the outputs \mathbf{t}_i are regular vectors of size d_o, not classes.
Let’s make the assumption that the underlying distribution is a multivariate normal distribution, with a mean vector \mu(\mathbf{x}) and standard deviation vector \sigma(\mathbf{x}) that depend on the input \mathbf{x}:
p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu(\mathbf{x}), \sigma(\mathbf{x}) \cdot I)
It is easy to generalize to anisotropic normal distributions with a full covariance matrix \Sigma(\mathbf{x}), but let’s keep the math simple here.
Our model will be a parameterized distribution p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}), which we can safely consider as a normal distribution too:
p_\theta (\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}) \cdot I)
The model is fully parameterized by the two vectors \mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}) and \sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}). All we need is a function approximator (aka neural network) taking \mathbf{x} as an input and returning the two vectors.
\mu_\theta, \sigma_\theta = F_\theta (\mathbf{x})
If we knew the original parameters \mu(\mathbf{x}) and \sigma(\mathbf{x}) of the data distribution, we would only need to minimize the KL (Closed form of the KL divergence for normal distributions):
\text{KL}(p ||p_\theta) = \log \dfrac{\sigma_\theta}{\sigma} + \dfrac{\sigma^2 + (\mu - \mu_\theta)^2}{2 \sigma_\theta^2} - \dfrac{1}{2}
As a side note, if we only care about the mean of the data (i.e. consider \sigma_\theta constant), the KL becomes proportional to:
\text{KL}(p ||p_\theta) \sim (\mu - \mu_\theta)^2
i.e. the squared difference between the mean prediction \mu_\theta and the mean of the data. Pretty close to the mse… Standard regression is just a sub-case of MVE where we do not care about the variance.
Anyway, we do not have access to the parameters of the data. All we can do is maximize the likelihood of our model on samples taken from the data distribution. It is the same as minimizing the negative log-likelihood:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{t} \sim p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x})} [- \log p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x})] \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p_\theta(\mathbf{t}_i | \mathbf{x}_i)
The NLL of a sample (\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{t}_i) is by definition of the normal distribution:
- \log p_\theta(\mathbf{t}_i | \mathbf{x}_i) = \dfrac{1}{2} [ \log 2 \pi + 2 \, \log \sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i) + \dfrac{(\mathbf{t}_i - \mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i))^2}{\sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i)^2}]
The loss function is a fully differentiable function of the parameters \theta: we can apply gradient descent (aka backpropagation) without any problem! Even if \mu_\theta(\mathbf{x}) and \sigma_\theta(\mathbf{x}) were the output of two different neural networks, we could train them in parallel by providing them the same loss function.

title: Mixture density networks for continuous distributions
text:
Mixture density networks
MVE is nice and all, as it allows to learn both the mean and variance of the data during regression, but it assumes that the data is normal, i.e. unimodal. In real life, interesting probability distributions are multimodal, which means that the pdf has more than one local maximum.






Figure 8.2: Unimodal vs. multimodal distributions. Source: https://medium.com/analytics-vidhya/learning-from-multimodal-target-mixture-density-network-94891d4e357e



In https://github.com/dusenberrymw/mixture-density-networks/blob/master/mixture_density_networks.ipynb, they take a nice example to understand why it is important. As seen on the left of Figure 8.3, it is very easy to do a non-linear regression y = f_\theta(x) on this data.






Figure 8.3: Left: the forward model y = f_\theta(x) is easy to regress. Right: the inverse model x = f_\theta(y) is not, as one value of y corresponds to several values of x. Source: https://github.com/dusenberrymw/mixture-density-networks



However, learning the inverse model x = f_\theta(y) is not possible for a regular regression algorithm, as the mean of x is not a function of y (one value of y can correspond to two values of x). The classical dataset for such a problem is the half-moon data, where the probability density of the y-axis is clearly multimodal:






Figure 8.4: Half-moons dataset (left) and the multimodal density of its y-coordinate (right).



For multimodal distributions, a mixture of Gaussians (as in the Gaussian Mixture Models - GMM - used in clustering) is able to approximate virtually any complex distribution. We just need a basis of K multivariate normal distributions \mathcal{N}(\mu_k(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) \cdot I) and weigh them with a mixing weight \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}):

    p_\theta(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathcal{N}(\mu_k(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) \cdot I)

The neural network should output for each component k:

the mean \mu_k(\mathbf{x}) of the component,
the std \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) of the component,
the weight \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}).

A necessary condition is that the weights \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}) are positive and sum to 1: \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}) = 1. A simple method to ensure this is to use a softmax over the corresponding output neurons z_k:

    \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}) = \dfrac{e^{z_k}}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}

Similarly, the std must be positive, so we take the exponential of the corresponding output neuron z^\sigma_k:

    \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) = e^{z^\sigma_k}







Figure 8.5: Architecture of a mixture density network. Source: https://medium.com/towards-data-science/predicting-the-unpredictable-905f634acc20



A mixture density network is a regular neural network outputting those three vectors for each component k. Training is done by maximizing the log-likelihood of the model on data samples, or equivalently by minimizing the loss function:

    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log p_\theta(\mathbf{t}_i | \mathbf{x}_i)  = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}_i) \cdot \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{t}_i; \mu_k(\mathbf{x}_i), \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}_i) \cdot I)

Because of the log of a sum, the loss does not simplify nicely, but it does not matter for pytorch or tensorflow: they can minimize it without a problem. It is straightforward to get the gradient of the loss with respect to \mu_k(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) (as in MVE) and \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}), and continue with backpropagation for the weights of the neural network.
After training, how do we use this network? For a given input \mathbf{x}, you would only get the value of the probability density function p_\theta of the mixture, which is not very informative unless you can visualize it.






Figure 8.6: Left: posterior density learned by a MDN. Right: means of the components, their size indicating their mixing weight. Source: https://gpflow.readthedocs.io/en/v1.5.1-docs/notebooks/tailor/mixture_density_network.html



Getting a sample out of the mixture requires two steps:

sample a component k using the softmax mixing weights \alpha_k(\mathbf{x}).
sample the corresponding normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu_k(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_k(\mathbf{x}) \cdot I).

Figure 8.7 shows an example with sampling from two components on the half-moons.






Figure 8.7: Sampling from a two-component MDN on the half-moons. Source: https://medium.com/@dave.cote.msc/made-easy-mixture-density-network-for-multivariate-regression-49e576721b3







Nix, D. A., and Weigend, A. S. (1994). Estimating the mean and variance of the target probability distribution. in Proceedings of 1994 IEEE international conference on neural networks (ICNN’94), 55–60.


Sluijterman, L., Cator, E., and Heskes, T. (2024). Optimal training of Mean Variance Estimation neural networks. Neurocomputing 597, 127929. doi:10.1016/j.neucom.2024.127929.

title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
Expectations everywhere
Nearly every quantity we manipulate in this book is a mathematical expectation over some probability distribution:

The entropy, the cross-entropy and the KL divergence (Information theory) are expectations of (log-)probabilities:


    H(X) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [- \log p(x)] \qquad \text{KL}(p || q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}]


The loss functions of machine learning are expectations over the data distribution, for example the negative log-likelihood (Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning):


    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [- \log p_\theta(x)]


The evidence of a latent variable model (see Latent variable models later) is an expectation over the prior of the latent variables:


    p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_\theta(z)} [p_\theta(x | z)]


The predictions of full Bayesian inference (Maximum a posteriori (MAP)) are an expectation over the posterior of the parameters:


    p(x | X) = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p(\theta | X)} [p(x | \theta)]


The ELBO of variational inference (see Variational inference later) is an expectation over an approximate posterior q_\phi(z|x).

All these quantities have the same generic form: the expectation of some function f(x) when x is distributed according to p(x), which is by definition an integral over all possible values of x:

    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] = \int_x f(x) \, p(x) \, dx

In the discrete case, the integral is replaced by a sum over all possible outcomes, but the problem is the same.


Closed forms are the exception
In a few lucky cases, this integral can be computed analytically. We saw two of them:

The KL divergence between two normal distributions only depends on their parameters (Closed form of the KL divergence for normal distributions).
The posterior of the mean of a normal distribution with a normal prior is itself a normal distribution (conjugate prior, Maximum a posteriori (MAP)).

As soon as a neural network is involved (the likelihood p_\theta(x) of a deep model, the decoder p_\theta(x|z) of a VAE, etc.), there is no hope of computing the integral analytically. We need to approximate it numerically.


Numerical integration does not scale
The classical way to approximate an integral numerically is quadrature: we cut the space of x into a regular grid, evaluate f(x) \, p(x) at each point of the grid, and sum the values weighted by the volume of each cell (Riemann sum). In one dimension, a grid of M = 100 points is usually enough to get a decent approximation.
The problem is that the number of points of the grid grows exponentially with the dimension d of x. If we keep M points per dimension, we need:

    M^d

evaluations of the function (Figure 9.1). With M=100 points per dimension:

d = 1: 100 evaluations.
d = 10: 10^{20} evaluations, already out of reach.
d = 784 (a small 28 \times 28 grayscale image): 10^{1568} evaluations, to be compared with the roughly 10^{80} atoms in the observable universe.







Figure 9.1: A regular grid with M = 10 points per dimension needs 10 points in one dimension, 100 in two dimensions and 1000 in three dimensions. Source: https://dibyaghosh.com/blog/probability/highdimensionalgeometry.html



This is the curse of dimensionality. Worse, most of these evaluations are wasted: in high dimensions, the probability mass of p(x) is concentrated in a tiny fraction of the space, so almost all grid points contribute nothing to the sum.


The idea of sampling
Monte Carlo methods take a radically different approach: instead of visiting the whole space systematically, we let the distribution tell us where to look. If we can draw N samples x_i from p(x), the expectation can be approximated by the average of f over the samples:

    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)

The samples automatically fall where the probability mass is: regions where p(x) is high are visited often, regions where it is negligible are almost never visited. No evaluation is wasted.






TipExample: computing \pi



The classical example of a Monte Carlo method is the computation of \pi. Let’s draw points x = (x_1, x_2) uniformly in the square [-1, 1]^2, whose area is 4. The disk of radius 1 centered on the origin lies inside the square and has an area of \pi. The probability that a point falls inside the disk is therefore the ratio of the two areas:

    P(||x|| \leq 1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}

This probability can be written as an expectation, using the indicator function \mathbb{I}(||x|| \leq 1), which is equal to 1 when the point is inside the disk and 0 otherwise:

    \pi = 4 \, P(||x|| \leq 1) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{U}([-1, 1]^2)} [4 \, \mathbb{I}(||x|| \leq 1)]

We are exactly in the setting above, with p(x) the uniform distribution on the square and f(x) = 4 \, \mathbb{I}(||x|| \leq 1). If N_\text{in} of the N samples fall inside the disk, the Monte Carlo approximation is:

    \pi \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N 4 \, \mathbb{I}(||x_i|| \leq 1) = 4 \, \dfrac{N_\text{in}}{N}







Figure 9.2: Monte Carlo estimate of \pi with N = 100, 1000 and 10000 points sampled uniformly in the square. The proportion of points inside the circle approximates \pi / 4.



As seen on Figure 9.2, the estimate gets closer to \pi = 3.14159\ldots when the number of samples increases, but rather slowly: with 10000 samples, the error is still around 0.003. How fast the estimate converges is the topic of the next section.


We already used this approximation several times without discussing it: to estimate the cross-entropy between the data and a model (Kullback-Leibler divergence in machine learning), or to replace the expectations of a loss function by an average over a minibatch of training data. This chapter looks at it more closely. It requires two things:

being able to evaluate f(x) for any x,
being able to draw samples from p(x).

The first requirement is usually easy. The second one is the difficult part, and the rest of the chapter is organized around it:

We first analyze the Monte Carlo estimator itself: why it works, and how fast it converges when we can sample from p(x).
We then see how to sample from simple distributions, for which dedicated methods exist.
When p(x) is too complex to be sampled directly, rejection sampling and importance sampling use a simpler proposal distribution q(x) instead.
Finally, we will see why these methods also break down in high dimensions, which motivates Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods in the next chapter.

title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
The Monte Carlo estimator

Definition
Let’s draw N samples x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N independently from p(x) (i.i.d., as in Maximum likelihood estimation). The Monte Carlo estimator of \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] is the sampling average of f:

    \hat{f}_N = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)

It is important to realize that \hat{f}_N is itself a random variable: if we draw another set of N samples, we obtain a different value. In the example of \pi, each panel of Figure 9.2 gave a different estimate, and repeating the experiment with other random points would give yet other values. The questions we need to answer are therefore statistical:

Is \hat{f}_N correct on average, i.e. is its expectation equal to the quantity we want?
How far from the true value is a single estimate likely to be, i.e. what is its variance?

To simplify the notations, let’s call \mu_f and \sigma_f^2 the mean and variance of f(x) when x \sim p(x):

    \mu_f = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] \qquad\qquad \sigma_f^2 = \text{Var}_{x \sim p(x)} (f(x)) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [(f(x) - \mu_f)^2]

\mu_f is the quantity we want to estimate. \sigma_f^2 measures how much the values of f fluctuate from one sample to another.


The estimator is unbiased
The expectation of the estimator (over all possible sets of N samples) is, by linearity of the expectation:

\begin{aligned}
    \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}_N] &= \mathbb{E}[\dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)] & \text{(Definition)} \\
    &= \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{x_i \sim p(x)}[f(x_i)] & \text{(Linearity of the expectation)} \\
    &= \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N \mu_f & \text{(All samples come from } p(x)) \\
    &= \mu_f & \\
\end{aligned}

On average, the Monte Carlo estimator gives exactly the right value: it is an unbiased estimator of \mu_f. Note that this holds for any number of samples, even N=1: a single sample f(x_1) is an unbiased (but very noisy) estimate of \mu_f.
This is what we do implicitly when we train a neural network with stochastic gradient descent: the gradient of the loss is estimated on a small minibatch of samples instead of the whole dataset. The estimate is noisy, but it is correct on average, which is enough for gradient descent to converge. Variational autoencoders (Variational autoencoders) even estimate the reconstruction loss with a single sample z \sim q_\phi(z|x) per input.


The variance decreases with N
The variance of the estimator tells us how much a single estimate deviates from \mu_f. Because the samples are independent, the variance of their sum is the sum of their variances. Moreover, multiplying a random variable by a constant a multiplies its variance by a^2:

\begin{aligned}
    \text{Var}(\hat{f}_N) &= \text{Var}(\dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)) & \text{(Definition)} \\
    &= \dfrac{1}{N^2} \, \text{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i)) & (\text{Var}(a X) = a^2 \, \text{Var}(X)) \\
    &= \dfrac{1}{N^2} \, \sum_{i=1}^N \text{Var}_{x_i \sim p(x)} (f(x_i)) & \text{(Independent samples)} \\
    &= \dfrac{1}{N^2} \, N \, \sigma_f^2 & \text{(All samples come from } p(x)) \\
    &= \dfrac{\sigma_f^2}{N} & \\
\end{aligned}

The standard deviation of the estimator, also called its standard error, is therefore:

    \sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat{f}_N)} = \dfrac{\sigma_f}{\sqrt{N}}

Moreover, as \hat{f}_N is a sampling average of i.i.d. variables, the central limit theorem (Bayesian estimation) tells us that it is approximately normally distributed for large N, whatever the distribution of f(x):

    \hat{f}_N \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_f, \dfrac{\sigma_f}{\sqrt{N}})

This allows to quantify the error of a single estimate: as for any normal distribution, \hat{f}_N falls within two standard errors of the true value \mu_f about 95% of the time.


Consequences
The formula \sigma_f / \sqrt{N} is the most important result of this chapter. Let’s look at what it means:

The error decreases as 1/\sqrt{N}. More samples always help, but slowly: to divide the error by 2, we need 4 times more samples; to gain one decimal (divide the error by 10), we need 100 times more samples. Monte Carlo methods are good at giving a rough estimate quickly, not at reaching a high precision.
The error does not depend on the dimension d of x. The dimension does not appear anywhere in the formula: estimating an expectation over a 784-dimensional space converges at the same rate 1/\sqrt{N} as in one dimension. This is the fundamental reason why sampling escapes the curse of dimensionality (Numerical integration does not scale), while the grid needed M^d points.
The constant \sigma_f matters. For a fixed budget of samples, the error is proportional to the standard deviation of f(x) under p(x). A function that fluctuates a lot between samples needs many more samples than a nearly constant one. This is where the dimension can come back in disguise: in high dimensions, \sigma_f itself can become very large. Reducing \sigma_f is the goal of variance reduction techniques, among which importance sampling (see below).

In practice, \sigma_f is unknown, as it is an expectation itself. But it can be estimated from the same samples, using the empirical variance:

    \sigma_f^2 \approx \dfrac{1}{N-1} \, \sum_{i=1}^N (f(x_i) - \hat{f}_N)^2

so that every Monte Carlo estimate can come with an estimate of its own error bar.






TipExample: convergence of the estimate of \pi



Let’s come back to the computation of \pi, where f(x) = 4 \, \mathbb{I}(||x|| \leq 1) takes the value 4 with probability \pi / 4 and 0 otherwise. Its mean is \mu_f = 4 \times \frac{\pi}{4} = \pi, as expected. As f(x)^2 takes the value 16 with probability \pi / 4, its variance is:

    \sigma_f^2 = \mathbb{E}[f(x)^2] - \mu_f^2 = 16 \, \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \pi^2 = \pi \, (4 - \pi) \approx 2.70

The standard error of the estimate is therefore:

    \dfrac{\sigma_f}{\sqrt{N}} \approx \dfrac{1.64}{\sqrt{N}}

With N = 10000 samples, the standard error is about 0.016: the error of 0.003 we obtained in Figure 9.2 was actually on the lucky side. To get 6 correct decimals, we would need an error around 10^{-6}, i.e. N \approx 2.7 \times 10^{12} samples…






Figure 9.3: Left: five independent runs of the Monte Carlo estimate of \pi as a function of the number of samples N (log-scale). The gray band shows one standard error \sigma_f / \sqrt{N} around \pi. Right: root mean square error of the estimate over 200 runs (log-log scale), compared to the theoretical standard error.



Figure 9.3 shows both aspects. On the left, each run fluctuates a lot for small N, then all runs converge towards \pi, staying most of the time within one or two standard errors. On the right, the measured error on a log-log scale is a straight line of slope -1/2, exactly following the theoretical 1.64 / \sqrt{N}.








TipExample: Monte Carlo estimate of the KL divergence



When the two distributions are not normal, the KL divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence) has no closed form. But it is an expectation over the first distribution:

    \text{KL}(p || q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[- \log \dfrac{q(x)}{p(x)}]

If we can sample from p(x) and evaluate both densities p(x) and q(x), the Monte Carlo estimator applies with f(x) = - \log \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}:

    \text{KL}(p || q) \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N - \log \dfrac{q(x_i)}{p(x_i)} \qquad \text{with} \qquad x_i \sim p(x)

In words: take samples from p, and average the log-ratio of their likelihoods under p and q (Figure 2.3). Note that individual terms of the sum can be negative (for samples where q(x_i) > p(x_i)), even though the KL itself is always positive: only the average is guaranteed to be correct. With few samples, the estimate can even be negative.
