title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
Sampling from simple distributions
The Monte Carlo estimator requires samples from p(x). But how does a computer actually produce a sample of a distribution? This section presents the basic tools, which work for simple distributions and serve as building blocks for the more complex methods of the next sections.

Everything starts from uniform numbers
Computers are deterministic machines: they cannot produce truly random numbers. Instead, they use pseudo-random number generators (PRNG), deterministic algorithms that produce a sequence of numbers that look random: they are uniformly distributed in [0, 1] and pass all statistical tests of independence. Numpy uses for example the PCG64 algorithm by default.
The sequence is entirely determined by its starting point, the seed. Using the same seed produces exactly the same sequence of numbers, which makes experiments reproducible: all the figures of this chapter are generated with a fixed seed.
Samples u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) of the uniform distribution are therefore the only randomness we have access to. Sampling any other distribution means transforming uniform samples. The simplest transformation is an affine one: if u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), then:

    x = a + (b - a) \, u \sim \mathcal{U}(a, b)

This is how we sampled points in the square [-1, 1]^2 for the computation of \pi, one coordinate at a time.


Inverse transform sampling
A general method to transform uniform samples into samples of a univariate distribution p(x) uses its cumulative distribution function (CDF):

    F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x p(x') \, dx'

The CDF increases monotonically from 0 to 1. If we can compute its inverse F^{-1}, sampling is straightforward:

sample u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1),
return x = F^{-1}(u).

Intuitively, u selects a “quantile” of the distribution uniformly: x is the value below which a fraction u of the probability mass lies. Regions where p(x) is high are regions where the CDF is steep, so a large interval of values of u is mapped onto a small interval of x: these values of x are obtained often.






NoteProof





We need to show that the CDF of x = F^{-1}(u) is F. For any value x, as F is monotonically increasing:

    P(F^{-1}(u) \leq x) = P(u \leq F(x)) = F(x)

where the last equality comes from the CDF of the uniform distribution: P(u \leq a) = a for any a \in [0, 1].



For example, the exponential distribution of rate \lambda, often used to model waiting times, has the pdf and CDF:

    p(x) = \lambda \, e^{- \lambda x} \qquad\qquad F(x) = 1 - e^{- \lambda x} \qquad\qquad \text{for } x \geq 0

Solving u = F(x) for x gives the inverse CDF, i.e. the sampling formula:

    x = F^{-1}(u) = - \dfrac{1}{\lambda} \, \log(1 - u)

Figure 9.4 illustrates the method. On the left, ten evenly spaced values of u are mapped through the inverse CDF: near x = 0, where the CDF is steep, they give closely packed values of x; in the tail of the distribution, where the CDF is flat, they give widely spread values. On the right, the histogram of 10000 samples obtained this way matches the pdf of the exponential distribution.






Figure 9.4: Inverse transform sampling of the exponential distribution with \lambda = 1. Left: evenly spaced values of u on the y-axis are mapped to x = F^{-1}(u) on the x-axis through the CDF. Right: histogram of 10000 samples compared to the pdf.



The method has two limitations:

It requires the inverse CDF in closed form, or at least a cheap way to compute it. Even for the normal distribution, the CDF has no closed form (it involves the error function).
It only works in one dimension: the CDF of a multivariate distribution cannot be inverted in general.



Normal distributions
The normal distribution is so important that dedicated methods exist. The Box-Muller transform turns two independent uniform samples u_1, u_2 \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) into two independent samples of the standard normal distribution:

    z_1 = \sqrt{-2 \log u_1} \, \cos(2 \pi u_2) \qquad\qquad z_2 = \sqrt{-2 \log u_1} \, \sin(2 \pi u_2)

We will not prove it here (it relies on a change of variables to polar coordinates). Libraries use faster variants, but the principle is the same.
Once we can sample from \mathcal{N}(0, 1), any normal distribution is an affine transformation away. If z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), then:

    x = \mu + \sigma \, z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)

In the multivariate case, if \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I) is a vector of independent standard normal samples and the covariance matrix is decomposed as \Sigma = L \, L^T (Cholesky decomposition), then \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{\mu} + L \, \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{\mu}, \Sigma). For a diagonal covariance matrix, this simply means \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{\mu} + \mathbf{\sigma} \odot \mathbf{z}, element-wise.
This is exactly the reparameterization trick of variational autoencoders (Variational autoencoders): instead of sampling the latent representation directly from q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{\mu_x}, \mathbf{\sigma_x}), we sample a noise vector from \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I) and transform it with the outputs \mathbf{\mu_x} and \mathbf{\sigma_x} of the encoder.


Categorical distributions
For a discrete distribution over K classes with probabilities p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_K (summing to one), inverse transform sampling takes a very simple form. We cut the interval [0, 1] into K consecutive segments of lengths p_1, \ldots, p_K, sample u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), and return the class whose segment contains u:

    k = \min \{ j \; | \; u \leq \sum_{i=1}^j p_i \}

Each class is selected with a probability equal to the length of its segment, i.e. p_k. This is how a class is sampled from the output of a softmax classifier (Softmax classifier for discrete distributions), how the component of a mixture density network is selected (Mixture density networks for continuous distributions), or how a language model samples the next token from its predicted distribution.


Ancestral sampling
The previous methods sample from distributions with a known, simple form. Many models are more complex, but they are built from simple distributions. A latent variable model (Latent variable models) defines the joint distribution of the latent variable z and the observation x as:

    p(x, z) = p(z) \, p(x | z)

where the prior p(z) and the conditional p(x | z) are simple (e.g. normal) distributions. To sample from the joint, we simply follow the generative process, “ancestors” first:

sample z \sim p(z),
sample x \sim p(x | z), with the value of z obtained in the first step.

The pair (z, x) is a sample of the joint distribution p(x, z). If we simply discard z, the remaining x is a sample of the marginal distribution:

    p(x) = \int_z p(x | z) \, p(z) \, dz

This is a remarkable property: we can sample from p(x) without ever computing this integral, which is intractable in general. This is how we sampled from a mixture density network (Mixture density networks for continuous distributions), where z is the index of the component, and how a trained VAE generates new images: sample \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I), then pass it through the decoder p_\theta(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z}).
The same principle applies to any model defined as a chain of conditional distributions, as long as each variable is sampled after the variables it depends on. Autoregressive models (Learning paradigms) are the extreme case: a language model samples the first token, then the second given the first, and so on:

    p(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_T) = p(x_0) \, \prod_{t=1}^T p(x_t | x_0, \ldots, x_{t-1})



When simple methods are not enough
Ancestral sampling illustrates an asymmetry that will follow us for the rest of the book:

For latent variable models, sampling from p(x) is easy, but evaluating p(x) for a given x is hard, as it requires the intractable integral over z.
For many other distributions, it is the opposite: we can evaluate the density, at least up to a constant, but we have no simple way to sample from it.

The second case is very common. The posterior of the parameters (Maximum a posteriori (MAP)) is known up to the evidence:

    p(\theta | X) = \dfrac{p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta)}{p(X)} \propto p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta)

We can evaluate the numerator for any \theta, but p(X) is intractable, and the posterior has no reason to be a simple distribution with a known sampling method. In general, we will only have access to an unnormalized density \tilde{p}(x):

    p(x) = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{Z} \qquad\qquad \text{with} \qquad Z = \int_x \tilde{p}(x) \, dx

where the normalization constant Z is unknown. The rest of this chapter (rejection and importance sampling) and the next one (MCMC) are about sampling from, or computing expectations under, such distributions.

title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
Rejection sampling

Principle
Let’s suppose that we want samples from a distribution p(x) = \tilde{p}(x) / Z, where we can evaluate the unnormalized density \tilde{p}(x) for any x, but do not know Z and have no direct way to sample from p(x).
Rejection sampling uses a simpler proposal distribution q(x) that we can sample from (for example a normal distribution), and a constant M large enough so that the scaled proposal M \, q(x) is above the target everywhere:

    \tilde{p}(x) \leq M \, q(x) \qquad \text{for all } x

M \, q(x) is called the envelope of the target. The algorithm then repeats the following steps:

sample a candidate x \sim q(x),
sample u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1),
accept x if u \leq \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{M \, q(x)}, otherwise reject it and start again.

The accepted samples are samples of p(x).
The method has a simple geometric interpretation (Figure 9.5, left). The pair (x, u \, M \, q(x)) is a point drawn uniformly under the curve of the envelope: x is distributed according to q(x), and its height is uniform between 0 and M \, q(x). The point is accepted if it also lies under the curve of the target \tilde{p}(x). The accepted points are therefore uniformly distributed under \tilde{p}(x), and their x-coordinates follow p(x): there are more accepted points where \tilde{p}(x) is high.






Figure 9.5: Rejection sampling of an unnormalized bimodal target \tilde{p}(x) (with Z=3) using the proposal q(x) = \mathcal{N}(0, 2) and M \approx 8.2. Left: each proposal x \sim q(x) is drawn at the height u \, M \, q(x); it is accepted if it falls under the target. Right: the histogram of the accepted samples matches the normalized target.









NoteProof





The probability density of proposing x and accepting it is the density of the proposal times the probability of acceptance:

    q(x) \times \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{M \, q(x)} = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{M}

Integrating over all x gives the overall probability of accepting a proposal:

    P(\text{accept}) = \int_x \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{M} \, dx = \dfrac{Z}{M}

The distribution of the accepted samples is the conditional distribution of x given acceptance, i.e. the ratio of the two:

    p(x | \text{accept}) = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x) / M}{Z / M} = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x)}{Z} = p(x)




Note that the unknown normalization constant Z is never needed: only \tilde{p}(x) is evaluated. The same holds for the proposal, which could also be unnormalized as long as we can sample from it.


Acceptance rate
The proof shows that a proposal is accepted with probability:

    P(\text{accept}) = \dfrac{Z}{M}

which is the ratio between the area under the target and the area under the envelope. All the rejected samples are wasted computations: on average, we need M / Z proposals to obtain one accepted sample. In Figure 9.5, about 37% of the proposals are accepted, as predicted.
The efficiency of rejection sampling therefore depends entirely on how well the envelope fits the target:

M should be as small as possible, i.e. the smallest value such that \tilde{p}(x) \leq M \, q(x) everywhere. Finding it requires knowing the maximum of \tilde{p}(x) / q(x), which is not always possible. If M is chosen too small, the condition is violated somewhere and the samples do not follow p(x) anymore, without any warning.
The proposal q(x) should have the same shape as the target. In particular, its tails must be at least as heavy as the tails of the target: if q(x) decreases faster than \tilde{p}(x) when x \rightarrow \infty, no constant M can satisfy the condition.

In Figure 9.5, most of the rejections happen between the two modes and in the tails, where the proposal puts mass that the target does not have.


Failure in high dimensions
Rejection sampling works well in one or two dimensions, but the acceptance rate collapses when the dimension increases. Let’s take a simple example, where both the target and the proposal are isotropic normal distributions centered on the origin in d dimensions, the proposal being slightly broader than the target:

    p(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_p^2 \, I) \qquad\qquad q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_q^2 \, I) \qquad\qquad \text{with } \sigma_q > \sigma_p

Both distributions are normalized (Z = 1). The ratio p(\mathbf{x}) / q(\mathbf{x}) is maximal at the origin, where it is equal to the ratio of the normalization constants of the two normal distributions:

    M = \max_\mathbf{x} \dfrac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} = \dfrac{p(\mathbf{0})}{q(\mathbf{0})} = (\dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p})^d

The acceptance rate is therefore:

    P(\text{accept}) = \dfrac{1}{M} = (\dfrac{\sigma_p}{\sigma_q})^d

It decreases exponentially with the dimension. Even if the proposal is only 1% broader than the target (\sigma_q = 1.01 \, \sigma_p), which is a nearly perfect fit, in d = 1000 dimensions:

    P(\text{accept}) = 1.01^{-1000} \approx 5 \times 10^{-5}

i.e. about 20000 proposals for a single accepted sample. In realistic problems, the proposal does not fit the target that well, and the acceptance rate is astronomically small: this is the curse of dimensionality (Numerical integration does not scale) again. Rejection sampling is therefore mostly used in low dimensions, for example as a building block inside other algorithms.
The fundamental problem is that all the rejected samples are thrown away, even though we evaluated \tilde{p}(x) for them. Importance sampling, presented in the next section, keeps all the samples but gives them different weights.

title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
Importance sampling

Principle
Rejection sampling throws away most of its proposals. Importance sampling takes a different approach: it keeps all the samples drawn from the proposal q(x), but corrects for the fact that they do not come from the target p(x) by giving each of them a weight.
Let’s first see the idea on Figure 9.6. We want the mean \mathbb{E}_p[x] of the target p(x), but we can only sample from the proposal q(x). If we simply average samples from q(x) (left), we obtain an estimate of the mean of q(x), not of p(x): most samples fall in a region where the target is negligible, and they pull the average towards the wrong value. Samples from q alone tell us nothing about p.
The solution is to give more importance to the samples that are likely under the target than to the ones that are not (right). A sample at x = -2 is frequent under q(x) but nearly impossible under p(x): it should count very little in the average. A sample at x = 2 is rare under q(x) but likely under p(x): it should count a lot, as it stands for all the samples of p(x) that q(x) fails to produce. With the right weights, the weighted average of the same samples estimates the mean of p(x).






Figure 9.6: Principle of importance sampling. The same 30 samples are drawn from the proposal q(x) in both panels. Left: their plain average estimates the mean of the proposal, not of the target. Right: when each sample is weighted by w(x) = p(x) / q(x) (marker area proportional to the weight), the weighted average (self-normalized, see below) estimates the mean of the target.



What are the right weights? Let’s derive them.
The trick is to introduce the proposal into the expectation, multiplying and dividing by q(x):

\begin{aligned}
    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] &= \int_x f(x) \, p(x) \, dx & \text{(Definition)} \\
    &= \int_x f(x) \, \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} \, q(x) \, dx & \text{(Introduce the proposal)} \\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q(x)} [\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} \, f(x)] & \text{(Expectation under the proposal)} \\
\end{aligned}

The ratio between the two densities is called the importance weight:

    w(x) = \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}

so that the expectation under the target becomes an expectation under the proposal of the weighted function:

    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q(x)} [w(x) \, f(x)]

The only requirement is that q(x) > 0 wherever f(x) \, p(x) \neq 0: the proposal must be able to produce every sample that matters for the target.
The right-hand side is an expectation under q(x), which we can sample from. The Monte Carlo estimator of The Monte Carlo estimator applies directly, giving the importance sampling estimator:

    \hat{f}_N^\text{IS} = \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N w(x_i) \, f(x_i) \qquad \text{with} \qquad x_i \sim q(x)

The weights correct for the mismatch between the two distributions, as on Figure 9.6. A sample in a region where the proposal is too generous (q(x) > p(x)) appears more often than it should under p(x), so its weight is smaller than 1. A sample in a region the proposal neglects (q(x) < p(x)) appears too rarely, so its weight is larger than 1.
As a plain Monte Carlo estimator of \mathbb{E}_q[w f], the importance sampling estimator inherits the properties of The Monte Carlo estimator: it is unbiased, and its variance is:

    \text{Var}(\hat{f}_N^\text{IS}) = \dfrac{\sigma_\text{IS}^2}{N} \qquad \text{with} \qquad \sigma_\text{IS}^2 = \text{Var}_{x \sim q(x)} (w(x) \, f(x))



Choosing the proposal
The estimator is unbiased for any proposal that covers the target, but its variance depends a lot on the choice of q(x). The weights w(x) = p(x) / q(x) give the intuition:

When the proposal is close to the target, all the weights are close to 1: every sample counts roughly the same, and importance sampling behaves like plain Monte Carlo sampling from p(x).
When the proposal is much smaller than the target in some region, the samples from that region are rare but receive huge weights. The estimate then depends on whether, and how many, such samples happen to be drawn.

A good proposal should therefore be as close as possible to the target and, as for rejection sampling, have tails at least as heavy as the target, so that no region of the target is neglected. A proposal that is too narrow produces two kinds of failures, illustrated on Figure 9.7 with the bimodal target of Figure 9.5:

Most of the time, no sample falls in the regions neglected by the proposal (run A, the second mode). The weights look perfectly reasonable, but the estimate ignores a part of the distribution and is wrong.
Occasionally, a sample falls in such a region and receives a huge weight, as q(x) \ll p(x) there (run B). This single sample then dominates the estimate.

The estimate jumps between these two situations from one run to another: this is what a large variance looks like.






Figure 9.7: Self-normalized importance sampling of the bimodal target with N = 50 samples. Top: target, proposal and samples. Bottom: normalized weights of the samples (note the different scales). Left: a broad proposal covering both modes gives balanced weights and a good estimate of \mathbb{E}_p[x] = -0.3. Middle and right: two runs of the same proposal centered on the first mode, too narrow to cover the second one. In run A, no sample reaches the second mode: the weights are nearly uniform, but the estimate is wrong. In run B, one sample reaches the second mode and receives 74% of the total weight.





Self-normalized importance sampling
Computing the weights w(x) = p(x) / q(x) requires the normalized target p(x). When we only know the unnormalized density \tilde{p}(x) = Z \, p(x) (Sampling from simple distributions), we compute the weights with \tilde{p}(x) instead, and normalize them so that they sum to one:

    \tilde{w}_i = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x_i)}{q(x_i)} \qquad\qquad \bar{w}_i = \dfrac{\tilde{w}_i}{\sum_{j=1}^N \tilde{w}_j}

The expectation is then approximated by the weighted average of the samples:

    \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] \approx \sum_{i=1}^N \bar{w}_i \, f(x_i)

The unknown constant Z multiplies all the weights by the same amount (\tilde{w}_i = Z \, w(x_i)), so it disappears in the normalization. This self-normalized importance sampling estimator is the one used in Figure 9.6 and Figure 9.7. It is slightly biased for a finite number of samples, but the bias vanishes when N increases.
As a by-product, the average of the unnormalized weights is an estimate of the normalization constant itself, as \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q(x)}[\tilde{w}(x)] = \int_x \tilde{p}(x) \, dx = Z:

    Z \approx \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{w}_i

This will be useful later: when Z is the evidence of a model, importance sampling provides an estimate of a quantity that is otherwise intractable.


Effective sample size
The normalized weights give a simple diagnostic of the quality of the estimate. If all weights are equal (\bar{w}_i = 1/N), every sample contributes equally, as in plain Monte Carlo sampling with N samples. If one weight is close to 1 and the others close to 0, the estimate relies on a single sample. The effective sample size (ESS) interpolates between these two extremes:

    \text{ESS} = \dfrac{(\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{w}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^N \tilde{w}_i^2} = \dfrac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^N \bar{w}_i^2}

It is equal to N when the weights are uniform and to 1 when a single sample carries all the weight. It can be interpreted as the number of samples from p(x) that would give an estimate of similar quality. In Figure 9.7, the broad proposal has an ESS of 34 out of 50 samples, while run B relies on fewer than 2 effective samples.






WarningThe ESS cannot see what the proposal misses



In run A of Figure 9.7, the ESS is 46 out of 50, better than with the good proposal, although the estimate is completely wrong. The ESS only measures how balanced the weights of the obtained samples are: it cannot detect regions of the target that the proposal never visits. A high ESS is necessary for a good estimate, but not sufficient.


Importance sampling is one of the most widely used tools of machine learning. In reinforcement learning, it allows to reuse samples collected with an older version of the policy to estimate quantities under the current one, as in the ubiquitous PPO algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017), used in robotics and in the alignment of large language models such as ChatGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022). Following the lesson of this section, PPO clips the importance weights to stay close to 1, so that the new policy never moves too far from the one that collected the samples. Importance-weighted autoencoders tighten the ELBO with several weighted samples of the encoder, and particle filters track hidden states over time with sequences of weighted samples: both will be presented in later chapters.

title: Monte Carlo and importance sampling
text:
Limits: towards MCMC

Importance sampling in high dimensions
We saw that rejection sampling collapses in high dimensions, as its acceptance rate decreases exponentially with the dimension (Rejection sampling). Importance sampling suffers from the same problem, in a different form: it keeps all the samples, but their weights become extremely unbalanced.
The reason is easy to see when the dimensions are independent, for example when the target and the proposal are both isotropic normal distributions. The densities are then products over the d dimensions, and so is the importance weight of a sample \mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_d):

    w(\mathbf{x}) = \dfrac{p(\mathbf{x})}{q(\mathbf{x})} = \prod_{k=1}^d \dfrac{p(x_k)}{q(x_k)}

Even if the proposal is close to the target, each factor is only roughly equal to 1: a bit larger for some samples, a bit smaller for others. A product of hundreds of such factors behaves very differently: a factor of 1.1 repeated 100 times gives 1.1^{100} \approx 14000, while a factor of 0.9 gives 0.9^{100} \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}. The weights of different samples therefore end up differing by many orders of magnitude, and the normalized weight of the luckiest sample gets close to 1: the effective sample size collapses.
Let’s take the example of Rejection sampling again: the target is \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_p^2 \, I) and the proposal \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_q^2 \, I) is 20% broader (\sigma_q = 1.2 \, \sigma_p). In this case, the fraction of effective samples \text{ESS} / N can be computed analytically. It is approximately:

In 100 dimensions, only one sample in 130 is effectively useful; in 1000 dimensions, no realistic number of samples gives a usable estimate. Real problems are much worse: the proposal is not a slightly broader copy of the target, and dimensions are counted in thousands or millions.


The problem with fixed proposals
Rejection sampling and importance sampling share the same weakness: the proposal q(x) is chosen once and for all, before seeing any sample, and must be good everywhere. In high dimensions, the probability mass of the target is concentrated in a tiny region of the space (Numerical integration does not scale). A fixed proposal that does not match this region almost perfectly wastes nearly all its samples, either by rejecting them or by giving them negligible weights. And we usually do not know where this region is: finding it is precisely the problem.


The idea of MCMC
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, presented in the next chapter, take a different route. Instead of drawing independent samples from a fixed global proposal, they build a chain of samples x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots, where each new sample is proposed locally, in the neighborhood of the current one:

If the proposed sample is more probable under the target, the chain moves there.
If it is less probable, the chain moves there only with some probability, and otherwise stays where it is.

Like rejection sampling, this only requires to compare the target at two points: the ratio \tilde{p}(x') / \tilde{p}(x) does not depend on the normalization constant Z, which cancels out. The chain progressively finds the regions of high probability and then wanders around them, spending in each region a time proportional to its probability. The price to pay is that successive samples are no longer independent: they carry partly redundant information, so the variance of the estimator is larger than the \sigma_f^2 / N of The Monte Carlo estimator.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Markov chains
The previous chapter ended on the limits of rejection and importance sampling: a proposal fixed once and for all cannot match a complex target in high dimensions. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods build samples one after the other, each new sample being proposed in the neighborhood of the current one. To understand why such a sequence of samples ends up following the target distribution, we first need a few notions about Markov chains.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Definition
A Markov chain is a sequence of random variables x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots in which each state only depends on the previous one, not on the rest of the history:

    p(x_{t+1} | x_t, x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_0) = p(x_{t+1} | x_t)

This is the Markov property: the chain is “memoryless”, the current state contains everything needed to predict the next one. The probability of moving from a state x to a state x' in one step is given by the transition kernel T(x' | x). We only consider chains where the transition kernel does not change over time.
Simulating a Markov chain is easy: start from an initial state x_0, then repeatedly sample the next state from the transition kernel, x_{t+1} \sim T(x' | x_t). When the states are discrete, this is just sampling from a categorical distribution (Sampling from simple distributions).
A classical toy example is the weather, with three possible states: sunny, cloudy and rainy. Each day, the weather of the next day is drawn according to the following transition probabilities (each row sums to one):

A sunny day is followed by another sunny day with probability 0.7, by a cloudy day with probability 0.2, and by a rainy day with probability 0.1. The left part of Figure 10.1 represents the same chain as a graph.






Figure 10.1: A Markov chain with three states. Left: transition probabilities. Middle: the distribution p_t(x) of the state at step t converges to the same stationary distribution, whether the chain starts on a sunny (solid lines) or a rainy day (dashed lines). Right: fraction of the time spent in each state by a single long chain, which converges to the stationary distribution (dotted lines).





Evolution of the distribution
If we know the state today, the state tomorrow is random. More generally, let’s call p_t(x) the probability that the chain is in state x at step t, i.e. the distribution we would observe over many independent runs of the chain. To be in state x' at step t+1, the chain must have been in some state x at step t and then moved from x to x'. Summing over all possible states x (law of total probability):

    p_{t+1}(x') = \sum_x T(x' | x) \, p_t(x)

In the continuous case, the sum becomes an integral:

    p_{t+1}(x') = \int_x T(x' | x) \, p_t(x) \, dx

Let’s start on a sunny day: p_0 = (1, 0, 0) for (sunny, cloudy, rainy). The next day, the distribution is given by the first row of the table: p_1 = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1). Applying the formula once more:

    p_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.7 \times 0.7 + 0.3 \times 0.2 + 0.2 \times 0.1 = 0.57

and similarly for the two other states, giving p_2 = (0.57, 0.26, 0.17). Repeating this, we get p_3 = (0.51, 0.29, 0.20), p_4 = (0.48, 0.30, 0.22), p_5 = (0.47, 0.30, 0.22)… The distribution changes less and less: the chain progressively forgets that it started on a sunny day.


Stationary distribution
The middle part of Figure 10.1 shows that the distribution converges towards fixed values, around (0.46, 0.31, 0.23), and that these values are the same if we start on a rainy day instead. Once the chain has reached this distribution, applying the transition kernel does not change it anymore. Such a distribution p(x) is called a stationary distribution of the chain:

    p(x') = \sum_x T(x' | x) \, p(x)

For the weather chain, we can check that p = (\frac{6}{13}, \frac{4}{13}, \frac{3}{13}) \approx (0.46, 0.31, 0.23) is stationary. For example, for the sunny state:

    0.7 \times \dfrac{6}{13} + 0.3 \times \dfrac{4}{13} + 0.2 \times \dfrac{3}{13} = \dfrac{4.2 + 1.2 + 0.6}{13} = \dfrac{6}{13}

In the long run, it is sunny 46% of the days, cloudy 31% and rainy 23%, whatever the weather on the first day.
This convergence is not specific to this example. If two mild conditions are satisfied:

every state can be reached from every other state in a finite number of steps (the chain is irreducible),
the chain does not cycle deterministically between groups of states (the chain is aperiodic),

then the chain has a unique stationary distribution, and p_t converges to it from any initial state. We will not prove this result here; see for example Bishop (2006) or MacKay (2003).


Time averages
The middle part of Figure 10.1 describes many independent runs of the chain. What happens with a single run? The right part of the figure shows the fraction of the days spent in each state by one long chain: it also converges to the stationary distribution. A single chain that runs long enough visits each state a fraction of the time equal to its stationary probability.
More generally, the average of any function f over the states visited by the chain converges to its expectation under the stationary distribution:

    \dfrac{1}{N} \, \sum_{t=1}^N f(x_t) \rightarrow \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} [f(x)] \qquad \text{when } N \rightarrow \infty

This is exactly the Monte Carlo estimator of The Monte Carlo estimator, except that the samples x_t are now the successive states of a chain instead of independent samples. The estimate still converges, but more slowly, as successive states are correlated: today’s weather tells us a lot about tomorrow’s.


Turning the problem around
In the usual study of Markov chains, the transition kernel T is given (the physics of the weather) and we want to find the stationary distribution. MCMC turns the problem around:

the target distribution p(x) = \tilde{p}(x) / Z is given, at least up to its normalization constant;
we design a transition kernel T whose stationary distribution is p(x), and which is easy to simulate.

We then simulate the chain for a long time, and use its successive states as (correlated) samples of p(x). The next section explains how to build such a transition kernel.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Detailed balance

Probability flows
To design a transition kernel T with a given stationary distribution p(x), we could try to satisfy the stationarity condition directly:

    p(x') = \sum_x T(x' | x) \, p(x) \qquad \text{for all } x'

This condition is easier to interpret in terms of flows of probability. The term p(x) \, T(x' | x) is the probability that, at stationarity, the chain is in state x and moves to x' at the next step: it is the flow of probability going from x to x'. As the chain must go somewhere after x', we have \sum_x T(x | x') = 1, so the left-hand side can be written p(x') = \sum_x p(x') \, T(x | x'), and stationarity becomes:

    \underbrace{\sum_x p(x) \, T(x' | x)}_{\text{flow into } x'} = \underbrace{\sum_x p(x') \, T(x | x')}_{\text{flow out of } x'} \qquad \text{for all } x'

For every state, the total flow coming in must equal the total flow going out. This is sometimes called global balance. Think of a crowd of people moving between the rooms of a building: the number of people in each room stays constant as long as, for every room, as many people enter as leave. Where they come from and where they go does not matter. People could, for example, all walk around the building in a loop A → B → C → A, without anybody ever walking back: the occupancy of the rooms would still be stationary.
Designing T with this condition is difficult: for every state x', it involves a sum (or an integral) over all the states of the space, which is exactly the kind of computation we want to avoid.


A local condition
Fortunately, there is a stronger condition that is much simpler to satisfy. A transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with respect to p(x) if, for every pair of states x and x':

    p(x) \, T(x' | x) = p(x') \, T(x | x')

Instead of balancing the total flows of each state, detailed balance requires that the flows are balanced for every pair of states: the flow from x to x' equals the flow from x' to x. In the analogy of the crowd, between every pair of rooms, as many people go one way as the other. This condition only involves two states at a time: there is no sum over the whole space anymore.
Detailed balance implies global balance, hence stationarity: summing both sides over x gives exactly the flow into x' on the left and the flow out of x' on the right:

    \sum_x p(x) \, T(x' | x) = \sum_x p(x') \, T(x | x') = p(x') \, \sum_x T(x | x') = p(x')

The converse is not true. In the loop A → B → C → A, the flow from A to B is positive, but there is no flow from B to A: detailed balance is violated, although the distribution is stationary. More generally, detailed balance requires every move to be possible in both directions: if T(x' | x) > 0, then T(x | x') > 0. Such chains are called reversible: at stationarity, a film of the chain looks statistically the same when played backwards, whereas a chain circulating in a loop has a preferred direction.
The weather chain of Markov chains satisfies detailed balance with respect to its stationary distribution p = (\frac{6}{13}, \frac{4}{13}, \frac{3}{13}). For each pair of states, the two flows are equal:








Pair of states
flow one way
flow the other way




sunny, cloudy
\frac{6}{13} \times 0.2 = \frac{1.2}{13}
\frac{4}{13} \times 0.3 = \frac{1.2}{13}


sunny, rainy
\frac{6}{13} \times 0.1 = \frac{0.6}{13}
\frac{3}{13} \times 0.2 = \frac{0.6}{13}


cloudy, rainy
\frac{4}{13} \times 0.3 = \frac{1.2}{13}
\frac{3}{13} \times 0.4 = \frac{1.2}{13}





Sufficient, but not necessary
Detailed balance is therefore a sufficient condition for stationarity, not a necessary one. The loop A → B → C → A is an extreme case (the chain is moreover periodic, so it does not converge), but the same happens with less extreme chains. Consider three states placed on a circle, and a chain that moves clockwise with probability 0.6 and counter-clockwise with probability 0.4. By symmetry, the uniform distribution p = (\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}) is stationary: each state receives as much probability as it gives away. But between two neighboring states, the clockwise flow \frac{1}{3} \times 0.6 is larger than the counter-clockwise flow \frac{1}{3} \times 0.4: probability keeps circulating around the circle, while the distribution stays the same.
For MCMC, we do not need to characterize all the chains that have p(x) as stationary distribution: it is enough to build one of them. Detailed balance is the design principle of most MCMC methods.


Why detailed balance suits MCMC
Detailed balance can be rewritten as a condition on the ratio of the transitions in both directions:

    \dfrac{T(x' | x)}{T(x | x')} = \dfrac{p(x')}{p(x)} = \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x')}{\tilde{p}(x)}

The last equality is the key: the ratio of the probabilities of two states does not depend on the normalization constant Z, which cancels out. To build a transition kernel satisfying detailed balance, we only need to evaluate the unnormalized target \tilde{p}(x), at two points at a time. The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, presented in the next section, does exactly that.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm

The algorithm
The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (Hastings, 1970; Metropolis et al., 1953) builds a Markov chain satisfying detailed balance in two steps: a proposal step, which suggests a new state, and an acceptance step, which corrects the proposal so that the chain has the right stationary distribution.
The proposal distribution q(x' | x) plays the same role as in rejection and importance sampling (Rejection sampling), except that it now depends on the current state x: it proposes a new state in the neighborhood of the current one. A typical choice is a normal distribution centered on the current state, q(x' | x) = \mathcal{N}(x, s), where the standard deviation s is the step size. Starting from an initial state x_0, the algorithm repeats the following steps:

sample a candidate x' \sim q(x' | x_t),
compute the acceptance probability:


    \alpha(x_t, x') = \min \left(1, \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x') \, q(x_t | x')}{\tilde{p}(x_t) \, q(x' | x_t)} \right)


sample u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1): if u \leq \alpha(x_t, x'), accept the candidate, x_{t+1} = x'; otherwise reject it and stay where we are, x_{t+1} = x_t.

The successive states x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots are (correlated) samples of p(x), once the chain has converged to its stationary distribution.
As announced in Detailed balance, the target only appears through the ratio \tilde{p}(x') / \tilde{p}(x_t): the normalization constant Z cancels out, and we only need to evaluate the unnormalized target \tilde{p}(x). This is exactly the situation of the posterior distributions of Sampling from simple distributions, whose numerator (likelihood times prior) is easy to evaluate but whose evidence is not.


The Metropolis rule
The ratio q(x_t | x') / q(x' | x_t) corrects for proposals that are asymmetric, i.e. that propose some moves more easily than the reverse moves. For the most common proposals, it simply disappears. A normal distribution centered on the current state is symmetric: the probability of proposing x' from x is the same as the probability of proposing x from x', as both only depend on the distance |x' - x|:

    q(x' | x) = \mathcal{N}(x' ; x, s) = \mathcal{N}(x ; x', s) = q(x | x')

With such a symmetric proposal, the acceptance probability reduces to the original rule of Metropolis et al. (1953):

    \alpha(x_t, x') = \min \left(1, \dfrac{\tilde{p}(x')}{\tilde{p}(x_t)} \right)

The algorithm is then called random-walk Metropolis, and its behavior is very intuitive:

if the candidate is more probable than the current state (\tilde{p}(x') \geq \tilde{p}(x_t)), it is always accepted: the chain always goes uphill;
if it is less probable, it is accepted with a probability equal to the ratio of the probabilities: a candidate half as probable as the current state is accepted half of the time, a candidate a thousand times less probable almost never.

Without the second rule, the chain would climb to the nearest mode and stay there, as an optimization algorithm would. Accepting some downhill moves is what allows the chain to explore the whole distribution, spending in each region a time proportional to its probability.


Rejected candidates are repeated
The acceptance step looks similar to rejection sampling (Rejection sampling), but there is an essential difference: when a candidate is rejected, the current state is repeated in the chain, x_{t+1} = x_t. It is not discarded, and the algorithm does not simply try again.
These repetitions are what gives each state its correct weight. A state of high probability is hard to leave: most candidates around it are less probable and get rejected, so the chain stays there for several steps, and the state appears several times in the chain. A state of low probability is left quickly. If we only kept the accepted candidates, the chain would spend as much “time” in the low-probability regions as in the high-probability ones, and its samples would not follow p(x).






NoteProof that Metropolis-Hastings satisfies detailed balance





We need to show that p(x) \, T(x' | x) = p(x') \, T(x | x') for every pair of states. When x' = x, both sides are equal, so let’s suppose x' \neq x. The only way to move from x to x' is to propose x' and to accept it, so the transition kernel is:

    T(x' | x) = q(x' | x) \, \alpha(x, x')

The flow from x to x' is then:

\begin{aligned}
    p(x) \, T(x' | x) &= p(x) \, q(x' | x) \, \min \left(1, \dfrac{p(x') \, q(x | x')}{p(x) \, q(x' | x)} \right) & \text{(} Z \text{ cancels, so we can use } p \text{ instead of } \tilde{p} \text{)} \\
    &= \min \left( p(x) \, q(x' | x), \; p(x') \, q(x | x') \right) & \text{(multiplying both terms of the min)} \\
\end{aligned}

This expression is symmetric in x and x': swapping the two states gives the same result. The flow from x' to x, p(x') \, T(x | x'), is therefore equal to the flow from x to x': detailed balance holds, and p(x) is a stationary distribution of the chain (Detailed balance).



The acceptance probability is in fact built for this: the minimum makes the flow from x to x' equal to the smaller of the two “proposal flows” p(x) \, q(x' | x) and p(x') \, q(x | x'). The direction with the larger proposal flow is slowed down by rejecting some of its moves, until both directions are balanced.


Example
Figure 10.2 applies random-walk Metropolis to the bimodal target of Figure 9.5, with the step size s = 1 and the initial state x_0 = 0. Only the unnormalized target \tilde{p}(x) (with Z = 3) is used.






Figure 10.2: Random-walk Metropolis on the bimodal target of Figure 9.5, with the proposal q(x'|x) = \mathcal{N}(x, 1). Left: the first 200 steps of the chain. Each rejected candidate (crosses) leaves the chain at the same position, creating a flat segment. Right: the histogram of a chain of 10000 steps matches the target.



The trace on the left shows the typical behavior of the chain:

it wanders around the first mode (x \approx -1.5) for about 140 steps, then moves to the second one (x \approx 1.5);
most rejected candidates fall in regions of low probability: in the tails, or in the valley between the modes;
rejections create flat segments, where the same state is repeated.

Over 10000 steps, 65% of the candidates are accepted, and the histogram of the chain matches the target (right). The average of the chain, -0.34, is close to the true mean \mathbb{E}_p[x] = -0.3.
Two things are visible in the trace, however. First, successive samples are strongly correlated: the chain moves by small steps, and stays in the same mode for many steps in a row (about 25 on average over the whole chain, 140 at the beginning of the trace). Second, the result depends on the step size s and on the initial state x_0. The next section discusses these practical aspects.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Using MCMC in practice
Metropolis-Hastings is guaranteed to produce samples of p(x) in the limit of infinitely long chains. With a finite chain, the quality of the estimates depends on choices that the algorithm leaves open: the step size of the proposal, the initial state, and the number of steps. This section discusses them on the bimodal target, with three different step sizes (Figure 10.3).






Figure 10.3: Random-walk Metropolis on the bimodal target with three step sizes, all chains starting in the tail at x_0 = 8. Left: first 1000 steps of the chain, the first 500 being discarded as burn-in (shaded). Middle: histogram of the chain after burn-in (9500 steps) against the target. Right: autocorrelation \rho_k of the chain after burn-in, as a function of the lag k.




Choosing the step size
The step size s of the random-walk proposal q(x' | x) = \mathcal{N}(x, s) controls a trade-off between the size of the moves and their acceptance:

Too small (s = 0.1, top row): the candidates are so close to the current state that their probability is almost the same, and nearly all of them are accepted (96%). But each move is tiny: the chain behaves like a random walk with small steps and explores the distribution very slowly. After 10000 steps, it has spent most of its time in the minor mode on the right, and the histogram does not match the target.
Too large (s = 50, bottom row): the candidates land anywhere, mostly far in the tails where the target is negligible, and nearly all of them are rejected (3%). The chain stays still for tens of steps, and the few accepted moves are large jumps.
Good (s = 3, middle row): the candidates are far enough to explore the distribution quickly, and close enough to be accepted reasonably often (42%). The chain jumps between the two modes all the time, and its histogram matches the target.

A high acceptance rate is therefore not a sign of a good sampler: it is often the sign of a too small step size. The usual rule of thumb is to tune the step size so that the acceptance rate is between 25% and 50%. In high dimensions, the optimal acceptance rate of random-walk Metropolis approaches 23% (Roberts et al., 1997). In practice, the step size is adapted during the burn-in period (see below) until the acceptance rate falls into this range.
Note that the step size s = 1 used in Figure 10.2 was a bit too small: its acceptance rate is higher (65%), but it produces about four times fewer effective samples than s = 3 (in the sense defined below).


Burn-in
The chain starts from an arbitrary initial state x_0, often far from the regions of high probability: in Figure 10.3, all chains start at x_0 = 8, deep in the tail of the target. The first states of the chain depend on this initial state, not on the target: the distribution p_t of the chain has not converged to its stationary distribution yet (Markov chains).
These first samples are therefore discarded: this is the burn-in (or warm-up) period. Its required length depends on how fast the chain converges. With the good step size, the chain reaches the target in a couple of steps; with the too small one, it needs hundreds of steps just to walk down from x_0 = 8 to the region of high probability. In practice, the burn-in length is chosen by looking at the trace: the chain should have “forgotten” its initial state, i.e. fluctuate around a stable level. Discarding a few hundred or thousand steps is common.


Correlated samples
After burn-in, the samples of the chain follow the target, but they are not independent: each state is close to the previous one, or even equal to it when a candidate is rejected. Two successive samples therefore carry partly the same information, and a chain of N steps is worth less than N independent samples.
The right column of Figure 10.3 measures this dependence with the autocorrelation of the chain: how similar two states k steps apart are, on a scale from 1 (identical) to 0 (unrelated). With the good step size, the similarity fades within a few steps. With the too large step size, it takes almost a hundred steps, as the chain repeats the same state for tens of steps. With the too small one, two states 200 steps apart are still strongly related.
The effective sample size (ESS) of the chain summarizes this: it is the number of independent samples that would give an estimate of the same precision. It has the same meaning as the effective sample size of importance sampling (Importance sampling). In Figure 10.3, the 9500 samples kept after burn-in are worth about 1600 independent samples with the good step size, 190 with the too large one, and only 8 with the too small one. The ESS is the number to look at when comparing samplers: a sampler that is twice as slow per step but produces three times more effective samples is the better one.






NoteAutocorrelation and effective sample size





The autocorrelation of the chain at lag k is the correlation between the states x_t and x_{t+k}:

    \rho_k = \dfrac{\text{Cov}(x_t, x_{t+k})}{\text{Var}(x_t)}

with \rho_0 = 1, and \rho_k = 0 for all k > 0 if the samples are independent. For N correlated samples, the variance \sigma_f^2 / N of the Monte Carlo estimator (The Monte Carlo estimator) becomes approximately (we admit this result):

    \text{Var}(\hat{f}_N) \approx \dfrac{\sigma_f^2}{N} \, \left(1 + 2 \, \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k \right)

This is the variance that N / (1 + 2 \sum_k \rho_k) independent samples would give, hence the effective sample size:

    \text{ESS} = \dfrac{N}{1 + 2 \, \sum_{k=1}^\infty \rho_k}

In practice, the autocorrelations are estimated from the chain itself, and the sum is truncated when they become negligible (in Figure 10.3, at the first negative value).



Some implementations keep only one state every k steps, which is called thinning. It saves memory, but does not add any information: the thinned chain is not worth more independent samples than the full one.


Multimodality and multiple chains
The too small step size illustrates the most dangerous failure of MCMC. A chain that moves by small steps can stay in one mode for a very long time, as crossing the low-probability valley between two modes requires many unlikely moves in a row. Nothing in its trace reveals this: the chain fluctuates around a stable level and looks converged. This is the same “missed mode” problem as with a too narrow importance sampling proposal (Importance sampling).
The standard diagnostic is to run several chains from different initial states and to compare their estimates. If they disagree, at least some of them have not explored the whole target. With the too small step size, chains started on different sides of the target indeed give very different estimates of the mean, while with the good step size they all agree. Probabilistic programming libraries automate this comparison.
Agreement between chains is, however, not a proof of convergence: if all chains start in the same mode, they can all miss the other ones.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Gibbs sampling

One coordinate at a time
Metropolis-Hastings needs a proposal distribution, whose step size must be tuned. Gibbs sampling (Geman and Geman, 1984) avoids this choice in multidimensional problems, by updating the coordinates of x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d) one at a time. Each coordinate x_k is sampled from its distribution given the current values of all the other coordinates, noted x_{-k}:

    x_k \sim p(x_k | x_{-k})

This distribution is called the full conditional of x_k. A complete pass over the coordinates is called a sweep:

sample x_1 \sim p(x_1 | x_2, x_3, \ldots, x_d),
sample x_2 \sim p(x_2 | x_1, x_3, \ldots, x_d), using the new value of x_1,
… and so on until x_d.

The state at the end of each sweep is a new sample of the chain. There is no acceptance step: every new value is kept.
Gibbs sampling is in fact a special case of Metropolis-Hastings, where the proposal changes only one coordinate, by sampling it from its full conditional. With this proposal, the acceptance probability is always exactly 1, which is why no candidate is ever rejected.






NoteProof that the acceptance probability is 1





Let’s consider the update of the coordinate x_k: the candidate x' is equal to x, except for its coordinate x'_k, which is sampled from q(x' | x) = p(x'_k | x_{-k}). As the other coordinates are unchanged, x'_{-k} = x_{-k}. Using p(x) = p(x_k | x_{-k}) \, p(x_{-k}), the ratio in the acceptance probability of Metropolis-Hastings is:

    \dfrac{p(x') \, q(x | x')}{p(x) \, q(x' | x)} = \dfrac{p(x'_k | x_{-k}) \, p(x_{-k}) \; p(x_k | x_{-k})}{p(x_k | x_{-k}) \, p(x_{-k}) \; p(x'_k | x_{-k})} = 1

All terms cancel: the candidate is always accepted. As Metropolis-Hastings satisfies detailed balance (The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm), each coordinate update leaves p(x) stationary, and so does a whole sweep.





When is it useful?
Gibbs sampling only makes sense when the full conditionals are easy to sample from, which happens more often than one might think: the joint distribution p(x) can be very complex, while each coordinate taken separately, all others being fixed, follows a simple distribution. This is typically the case in models built from simple conditional distributions:

in Bayesian models with conjugate priors (Maximum a posteriori (MAP)), the conditional distribution of each parameter, given the data and the other parameters, is a known distribution;
in latent variable models (Latent variable models), we can alternate between sampling the latent variables given the parameters, and the parameters given the latent variables.

Gibbs sampling was originally introduced for image restoration (Geman and Geman, 1984), where each pixel only depends on its neighbors, and was for a long time the workhorse of Bayesian statistics.


Example: correlated coordinates
Let’s apply Gibbs sampling to a bivariate normal distribution, with zero mean, unit variances and correlation \rho. Its full conditionals are one-dimensional normal distributions (we admit this result):

    p(x_1 | x_2) = \mathcal{N}(\rho \, x_2, \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}) \qquad p(x_2 | x_1) = \mathcal{N}(\rho \, x_1, \sqrt{1 - \rho^2})

Each update moves the chain parallel to one axis: horizontally when x_1 is updated, vertically when x_2 is. Figure 10.4 shows the path of the chain in two cases.






Figure 10.4: Gibbs sampling of a bivariate normal distribution with unit variances, starting from (-3, -3), for 30 sweeps. The blue ellipses delimit 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. Each update moves the chain parallel to one axis. Left: uncorrelated coordinates. Right: strongly correlated coordinates.




When the coordinates are independent (\rho = 0, left), each conditional is the full distribution of the coordinate: every sweep produces an independent sample, wherever the chain was before. The first sweep immediately brings the chain from its initial state to the center of the distribution.
When the coordinates are strongly correlated (\rho = 0.95, right), the conditionals are very narrow: once x_2 is fixed, x_1 can only change a little, and vice versa. The chain can only move along the diagonal of the distribution with small, staircase-like steps, and successive samples are strongly correlated.

This is the main limitation of Gibbs sampling: it explores the distribution efficiently only when the coordinates are weakly dependent. Strong dependencies, which are common in practice (for example between the parameters of a model), make it as slow as a random walk with a too small step size. Grouping strongly correlated coordinates and sampling them jointly (blocked Gibbs sampling) reduces the problem, when their joint conditional is still simple.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Example: sampling a posterior
Let’s go back to the Bayesian estimation of the parameters of a normal distribution (Maximum a posteriori (MAP)). To keep the math simple, the MAP example assumed that the standard deviation \sigma of the data was known, and chose a normal prior for the mean \mu, so that the posterior was a normal distribution. Let’s now estimate both parameters \theta = (\mu, \sigma) from N = 20 samples X = \{x_i\} of \mathcal{N}(3, 2), with priors that are not conjugate: a broad normal prior \mathcal{N}(0, 5) for \mu, and a broad half-normal prior for \sigma (a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 5) restricted to positive values).
The posterior has no simple closed form, but its unnormalized version, the likelihood times the prior, is easy to evaluate for any (\mu, \sigma):

    \tilde{p}(\mu, \sigma | X) = p(X | \mu, \sigma) \, p(\mu) \, p(\sigma) = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{N}(x_i ; \mu, \sigma) \; \mathcal{N}(\mu ; 0, 5) \; p(\sigma)

This is all Metropolis-Hastings needs: the evidence p(X) is never computed. With only two parameters, we could still normalize the posterior numerically on a grid, but the same code would work with hundreds of parameters, where no grid is possible (Numerical integration does not scale).
We use random-walk Metropolis in the two-dimensional space of the parameters, with the proposal \mathcal{N}((\mu, \sigma), 0.7) (the same step size in both directions), during 20000 steps after a burn-in of 1000 steps. Candidates with a negative standard deviation have a probability of zero under the prior: they are simply always rejected.
One practical detail matters: the likelihood is a product of N densities, which quickly becomes too small to be represented by floating-point numbers. The acceptance test is therefore computed in the log domain, by comparing \log u with the difference \log \tilde{p}(\mu', \sigma' | X) - \log \tilde{p}(\mu, \sigma | X), where the log-likelihood is a sum instead of a product, as in Maximum likelihood estimation.
The left part of Figure 10.5 shows the samples of the chain. Instead of a single point estimate, we get the whole posterior distribution of the parameters, and in particular how uncertain they are: with 20 data points, the mean is somewhere between about 1.8 and 3.5, and the standard deviation between 1.3 and 2.6. Any other quantity is a simple Monte Carlo average over the chain: the posterior mean of a parameter is the average of its samples, the probability that \mu > 3 is the fraction of the samples where this is true, and so on.






Figure 10.5: Bayesian estimation of the mean and standard deviation of a normal distribution from 20 data points, with random-walk Metropolis. Left: samples of the posterior p(\mu, \sigma | X) (one every ten steps) and their marginal histograms. Right: the posterior predictive distribution (blue) is the average of the normal densities \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t) of all the samples of the chain (a few of them in green).



The same holds for the posterior predictive distribution, which was out of reach in Maximum a posteriori (MAP). It is an expectation over the posterior:

    p(x | X) = \int p(x | \mu, \sigma) \, p(\mu, \sigma | X) \, d\mu \, d\sigma = \mathbb{E}_{(\mu, \sigma) \sim p(\mu, \sigma | X)} [\mathcal{N}(x ; \mu, \sigma)]

and is therefore estimated by averaging the normal densities corresponding to all the samples (\mu_t, \sigma_t) of the chain:

    p(x | X) \approx \dfrac{1}{T} \, \sum_{t=1}^T \mathcal{N}(x ; \mu_t, \sigma_t)

The right part of Figure 10.5 shows the result. Each sample of the chain is a plausible normal distribution for the data; their average is broader than each of them, as it also takes into account our uncertainty about the parameters. With more data, the posterior would become narrower, and the predictive distribution would get closer to a single normal distribution.
This example is small, but it contains the whole workflow of Bayesian inference with MCMC: write down the unnormalized posterior (likelihood times prior), sample it with a Markov chain, and compute any quantity of interest as an average over the chain.

title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
text:
Limits: towards gradient-based samplers
Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling solve the main problem of the previous chapter: they do not need a global proposal matching the whole target, only local moves and the ability to evaluate \tilde{p}(x). Their weakness is that these local moves are blind: a random-walk proposal draws candidates in random directions, without using any information about the shape of the target, and the acceptance step only corrects them afterwards.
In a few dimensions, this is not a problem, as a reasonable fraction of the random directions leads to regions of high probability. In high dimensions, almost all random directions lead away from the small region where the probability mass is concentrated (Numerical integration does not scale): a large step is then almost certainly rejected. To keep a reasonable acceptance rate, the step size must shrink when the dimension increases, and the chain explores the target with smaller and smaller steps. As for a random walk, the distance travelled only grows with the square root of the number of steps, so the number of steps needed to explore the target grows with the dimension. Gibbs sampling has the same problem as soon as the coordinates are correlated (Gibbs sampling), and it additionally requires simple conditional distributions.
The solution is to propose moves that follow the shape of the target. The gradient of the log-density \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x) points, at each state, in the direction where the probability increases fastest. Like the ratio \tilde{p}(x') / \tilde{p}(x), it does not depend on the normalization constant, as \log Z is a constant whose gradient is zero:

    \nabla_x \log p(x) = \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x) - \nabla_x \log Z = \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x)

Moving along the gradient, plus some noise to keep exploring, is the idea of Langevin dynamics; simulating the motion of a particle on the landscape of the log-density is the idea of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Both methods make large moves that are nevertheless accepted with a high probability, and scale much better with the dimension. They are presented in the next chapter. The gradient of the log-density, called the score, will also be at the heart of score-based diffusion models.

title: Langevin dynamics and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
The score
The previous chapter ended on the main weakness of Metropolis-Hastings: its random-walk proposals are blind, and explore the target more and more slowly when the dimension increases (Limits: towards gradient-based samplers). This chapter presents two samplers that use the gradient of the log-density to propose moves that follow the shape of the target: Langevin dynamics and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The gradient of the log-density will also be the central quantity of score-based diffusion models.
The gradient of the log-density with respect to x is called the score of the distribution:
\nabla_x \log p(x)
It is a vector with the same dimension as x, which points, at each state, in the direction where the log-density increases the fastest. As seen in Limits: towards gradient-based samplers, it does not depend on the normalization constant: \nabla_x \log p(x) = \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x), as \log Z is a constant whose gradient is zero. Like the acceptance ratio of Metropolis-Hastings, the score can therefore be computed from the unnormalized target only.
For a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma), the log-density is \log p(x) = - \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2 \sigma^2} + \text{cst}, so its score is:
\nabla_x \log p(x) = - \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma^2}
The score acts like a spring pulling x back towards the mean \mu: it is zero at the mean, and its strength increases linearly with the distance to the mean. The narrower the distribution (small \sigma), the stiffer the spring.
For the bimodal target of the previous chapters (Figure 11.1, left), the score points towards the nearest mode: it is positive on the left of each mode (go right) and negative on its right (go left). It is zero at the two modes, but also at the bottom of the valley between them: a zero score only means that the density is flat locally, not that it is high. The right part of the figure shows the same behavior in two dimensions, for a mixture of two Gaussians: the score is a vector field, whose arrows point towards the modes, and become longer far away from them.
Following the arrows of the score from any initial state leads to a mode: this is gradient ascent on the log-density, the method we would use to find the MAP estimate of Maximum a posteriori (MAP). To sample the distribution instead of finding its modes, we need to add noise to these moves, which is the topic of the next section.
The score of a simple distribution can be derived by hand, as above. For more complex models, for example when the likelihood involves a neural network, it is computed by automatic differentiation, exactly like the gradient of a loss function during training. This requires the target to be differentiable with respect to x: gradient-based samplers only apply to continuous variables.

title: Langevin dynamics and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
Langevin dynamics
Langevin dynamics adds noise to gradient ascent on the log-density. Starting from an initial state x_0, each step moves the state a little in the direction of the score, then adds some Gaussian noise:

    x_{t+1} = x_t + \epsilon \, \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x_t) + \sqrt{2 \epsilon} \, \xi_t \qquad \text{with } \xi_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)

where \epsilon is a small step size. The two terms have opposite effects:

without the noise, this is gradient ascent on \log p(x): the state converges to the nearest mode, i.e. to a MAP estimate (Maximum a posteriori (MAP));
without the score, this is a random walk with steps of standard deviation \sqrt{2 \epsilon}, which spreads the state everywhere.

The score concentrates the states around the modes, the noise spreads them. The factor \sqrt{2 \epsilon} is exactly the amount of noise for which the two effects balance, so that the stationary distribution of the chain is the target p(x). We admit this result, which comes from physics: the equation describes the motion of a particle in a potential - \log p(x), shaken by thermal noise, whose positions end up distributed according to p(x).
Figure 11.2 shows 400 independent Langevin chains on the 2D mixture of Figure 11.1, starting on a regular grid. Within about ten steps, the score brings the chains to the regions of high probability. They do not collapse onto the modes, though: the noise keeps them spread around each mode, as samples of the target should be. As in Markov chains, the snapshots show the distribution p_t of the chain at different steps, which converges to the target.






Figure 11.2: 400 independent Langevin chains on the 2D mixture of two Gaussians of Figure 11.1, with \epsilon = 0.05, starting on a regular grid. Inspired by the animation of https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/.



Compared to random-walk Metropolis, every step goes in a sensible direction, and there is no rejection: Langevin dynamics does not waste computations on candidates that would be rejected. The price to pay is a small error. The stationary distribution is exactly p(x) only in the limit of infinitely small steps; with a finite step size \epsilon, it is a slightly distorted version of the target. Reducing \epsilon reduces the error, but the chain then needs more steps to explore the target.
The Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA) (Roberts and Tweedie, 1996) removes this error by combining the two methods: the Langevin step is used as the proposal of Metropolis-Hastings, whose acceptance step corrects the distortion. The proposal is a normal distribution centered on the Langevin update:

    q(x' | x) = \mathcal{N}(x + \epsilon \, \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x), \sqrt{2 \epsilon})

Unlike the random-walk proposal of The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, this proposal is not symmetric: from a state x on the side of a mode, it favors moves towards the mode, and the reverse move is less likely to be proposed. This is precisely the situation for which Hastings introduced the correction q(x_t | x') / q(x' | x_t) in the acceptance probability. With a small step size, nearly all candidates are accepted, and MALA behaves like Langevin dynamics without its error.
Langevin dynamics is also used to sample the posterior over the weights \theta of a neural network (Bayesian deep learning). The score of the posterior p(\theta | X) \propto p(X | \theta) \, p(\theta) with respect to the weights is the gradient of the log-likelihood plus the gradient of the log-prior, i.e. exactly the gradient used to train the network with MAP (Maximum a posteriori (MAP)). A Langevin step is then a gradient step on the training loss plus some noise. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) (Welling and Teh, 2011) estimates this gradient on minibatches, as stochastic gradient descent does: with a decreasing step size, training the network with the right amount of noise produces samples of the posterior instead of a single set of weights.

title: Langevin dynamics and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
text:
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

A ball rolling on the landscape
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) (Duane et al., 1987; Neal, 2012) borrows its idea from physics. Let’s define the potential energy of a state as minus its log-density:

    U(x) = - \log \tilde{p}(x)

The regions of high probability become the valleys of an energy landscape, the modes being at the bottom of the valleys. Langevin dynamics moves a particle on this landscape as if it was in honey: it slides slowly downhill, shaken by the noise. HMC instead launches a ball without friction: given a random push, the ball rolls down into a valley, gaining speed, climbs up the other side, and keeps going. In a single trajectory, it can travel a long way across the region of high probability.
To describe this motion, HMC adds to each state x a momentum v (the velocity of the ball), of the same dimension as x. The ball has a kinetic energy K(v) = \frac{1}{2} ||v||^2, and its total energy is the Hamiltonian:

    H(x, v) = U(x) + K(v)

The laws of physics (Hamilton’s equations) state that the position changes with the momentum, and the momentum with the force, which is minus the gradient of the potential energy, i.e. the score:

    \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v \qquad \dfrac{dv}{dt} = - \nabla_x U(x) = \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x)

Without friction, the total energy H(x, v) is conserved along the trajectory: the ball converts potential energy into kinetic energy when it goes down, and back when it goes up.
How does this help to sample p(x)? HMC samples the pair (x, v) from the joint distribution:

    p(x, v) \propto \exp(- H(x, v)) = \tilde{p}(x) \, \exp(- \frac{1}{2} ||v||^2)

In this distribution, x and v are independent: x follows the target, and v a standard normal distribution. If we can sample pairs (x, v), we simply drop the momentum and keep x, which is a sample of the target (the same trick as ancestral sampling in Sampling from simple distributions, where we dropped the latent variable). And as H(x, v) is conserved along the trajectory, so is the density p(x, v): moving the ball along its trajectory does not change the probability of the pair, even though the position can change a lot.


The algorithm
Each iteration of HMC consists of the following steps, starting from the current state x_t:

sample a new momentum v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1): this is the random push, which sets the energy level of the trajectory;
simulate the motion of the ball during L small time steps of size \epsilon, using the leapfrog integrator, which gives a candidate (x', v');
accept the candidate with the probability \min(1, \exp(H(x_t, v) - H(x', v'))), otherwise stay at x_{t+1} = x_t;
drop the momentum.

If the motion was simulated exactly, the energy would be conserved and the candidate always accepted. The leapfrog integrator only simulates it approximately, so the energy changes a little: the acceptance step of Metropolis-Hastings corrects this error, as for MALA. With a small step size, the error is small and nearly all candidates are accepted.






NoteThe leapfrog integrator





Each leapfrog step updates the momentum and the position in turn, using the score at the current position:

\begin{aligned}
    v &\leftarrow v + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \, \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x) & \text{(half step on the momentum)} \\
    x &\leftarrow x + \epsilon \, v & \text{(full step on the position)} \\
    v &\leftarrow v + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \, \nabla_x \log \tilde{p}(x) & \text{(half step on the momentum, at the new position)} \\
\end{aligned}

Each step requires one evaluation of the score, so an iteration of HMC costs L gradient evaluations. The leapfrog integrator is preferred to simpler methods because it has two properties that make the acceptance probability above correct without any additional Hastings ratio: it is reversible (running it backwards from (x', -v') brings back (x, -v)), and it preserves volumes in the (x, v) space. We admit these results; see Neal (2012) for details.



Figure 11.3 compares HMC with random-walk Metropolis and Gibbs sampling on the correlated normal distribution of Figure 10.4. The first trajectory of HMC brings the chain from its initial state to the center of the distribution in a single iteration, and the following samples are spread over the whole distribution, almost independently of each other. Random-walk Metropolis and Gibbs sampling are still crawling along the diagonal. The comparison is not entirely fair, as each iteration of HMC costs 15 gradient evaluations. Counted per evaluation, HMC still produces several times more effective samples than the two other methods, and the gap widens quickly in higher dimensions.






Figure 11.3: 30 iterations of random-walk Metropolis, Gibbs sampling and HMC on the correlated normal distribution of Figure 10.4, from the same initial state. For HMC, the first three leapfrog trajectories are drawn; each iteration uses L = 15 leapfrog steps.





Tuning HMC
HMC has two parameters:

The step size \epsilon controls the accuracy of the simulation. Too large, and the energy is badly conserved, so that many candidates are rejected; too small, and many steps are needed to travel the same distance.
The number of steps L controls the length of the trajectories. Too short, and HMC loses its advantage: with a single leapfrog step, HMC is actually equivalent to MALA. Too long, and the trajectory makes a U-turn and comes back towards its starting point, wasting computations.

The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) (Hoffman and Gelman, 2011) removes the need to choose L: it extends each trajectory until it starts to turn back, and adapts the step size during the burn-in period. NUTS is the default sampler of probabilistic programming libraries such as Stan, PyMC or NumPyro, where the user only writes the model, and the gradients are computed by automatic differentiation. Betancourt (2017) gives a very intuitive introduction to the geometry behind HMC.

section: Limits and the bridge to diffusion models
text:
Limits and the bridge to diffusion models

Limits of gradient-based samplers
Using the score makes a huge difference in high dimensions. To obtain a new independent sample, the number of steps needed grows roughly like the dimension d for random-walk Metropolis, but only like d^{1/3} for MALA and d^{1/4} for HMC (Neal, 2012; Roberts et al., 1997). This is why HMC (with NUTS) is today the method of choice to sample posterior distributions with thousands of parameters.
Gradient-based samplers keep two limitations, however:

They are still local methods. The score points towards the nearest mode, so the valleys between distant modes remain difficult to cross. In Figure 11.2, the chains starting on the grid first split equally between the two modes, while the target puts 60% of its mass in the lower-left one: the correct proportions are only restored very slowly, by the few chains that manage to cross the valley. Methods such as tempering, which run additional chains on flattened versions of the target, help with this problem, but multimodal distributions remain the hardest case for MCMC.
They require a differentiable target: they do not apply to discrete variables, such as the categories of a classifier or the tokens of a language model.



Learning the score
There is one more observation to make about Langevin dynamics: it only needs the score \nabla_x \log p(x), never the density p(x) itself. Until now, we always assumed that the unnormalized target \tilde{p}(x) was known, for example a likelihood times a prior. In generative modeling (Learning paradigms), the situation is different: we have data, samples x_i of an unknown distribution p(x), for example images, and want to generate new samples of the same distribution.
If we could learn the score of the data distribution with a neural network s_\theta(x) \approx \nabla_x \log p(x), Langevin dynamics would use this learned score to generate new samples, without ever knowing p(x). This is the idea of score-based generative models (Song and Ermon, 2020) (Figure 11.4). Learning the score from data is possible with methods called score matching, which, conveniently, never require the normalization constant either.






Figure 11.4: Score-based generative modeling: the score of the data distribution is learned from data samples (score matching), and Langevin dynamics uses the learned score to generate new samples. Source: https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/.



A naive application of this idea does not work well, for two reasons:

The learned score is only accurate where there is data, i.e. close to the modes (Figure 11.5). In the low-probability regions between and around the modes, where Langevin chains usually start, the network has seen almost no data, and its score is unreliable.
The data distribution is extremely multimodal (think of all possible images), and we saw above that Langevin dynamics struggles to distribute the samples correctly between distant modes.







Figure 11.5: The learned score (right) is only accurate in the regions of high probability, where there is enough data to learn it; it is inaccurate elsewhere. Source: https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/.



The solution is to add noise to the data. Perturbing the data with a lot of Gaussian noise spreads it over the whole space: the score of the noisy distribution can be learned everywhere, and its modes are merged into a single smooth bump. Learning the score at several noise levels, and running Langevin dynamics while progressively decreasing the noise, guides the chains from anywhere in the space towards the data, while distributing them correctly between the modes. This is the principle of diffusion models, which will be presented in a later part of this book.
