section: Training: the ELBO of a hierarchical VAE
text:
Training: the ELBO of a hierarchical VAE

The evidence lower bound
As for any latent variable model, we would like to maximize the log-likelihood \log p_\theta(x_0) of the data under the model, but it requires integrating over all the latent variables x_1, \ldots, x_T, which is intractable. And as for the VAE, we can maximize instead the evidence lower bound of Variational inference, using the forward process as the encoder:

    \log p_\theta(x_0) \geq \mathbb{E}_{x_{1:T} \sim q(x_{1:T} | x_0)} [\log \dfrac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T} | x_0)}] = \text{ELBO}(\theta)

where p_\theta(x_{0:T}) = p(x_T) \, \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t) is the joint distribution of the reverse process, and q(x_{1:T} | x_0) = \prod_{t=1}^T q(x_t | x_{t-1}) the one of the forward process. As the encoder has no parameters, the ELBO only depends on the parameters \theta of the network. Thanks to the Markov structure of both processes, the ELBO decomposes into a sum of simple terms (Ho et al., 2020; Luo, 2022):

    \text{ELBO}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{q} [\log p_\theta(x_0 | x_1)] - \text{KL}(q(x_T | x_0) || p(x_T)) - \sum_{t=2}^T \mathbb{E}_{q} [\text{KL}(q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) || p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t))]







NoteDerivation





The ratio inside the ELBO is:

    \dfrac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T} | x_0)} = \dfrac{p(x_T) \, \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t)}{\prod_{t=1}^T q(x_t | x_{t-1})}

For t \geq 2, the forward steps can be reversed with Bayes’ rule conditioned on x_0 (the Markov property gives q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = q(x_t | x_{t-1}, x_0)):

    q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = \dfrac{q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) \, q(x_t | x_0)}{q(x_{t-1} | x_0)}

In the product over t = 2, \ldots, T, the fractions q(x_t | x_0) / q(x_{t-1} | x_0) cancel each other except the first and the last ones (a telescoping product), leaving q(x_T | x_0) / q(x_1 | x_0). The ratio becomes:

    \dfrac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T} | x_0)} = \dfrac{p(x_T)}{q(x_T | x_0)} \, p_\theta(x_0 | x_1) \, \prod_{t=2}^T \dfrac{p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t)}{q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0)}

Taking the logarithm and the expectation over the forward process, each ratio of the product gives minus a KL divergence, which leads to the decomposition.



The three kinds of terms have simple interpretations:

\text{KL}(q(x_T | x_0) || p(x_T)) compares the end of the forward process with the prior \mathcal{N}(0, I). It does not depend on \theta, and it is close to zero when \bar{\alpha}_T \approx 0: it can be ignored.
\log p_\theta(x_0 | x_1) is a reconstruction term for the very last denoising step, as in a VAE.
Each \text{KL}(q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) || p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t)) compares one learned reverse step with the reverse step knowing the data of the previous section. These are the terms that train the network: each reverse step should do what we would do if we knew the original sample.



From KL divergences to a simple regression
All the KL terms are divergences between two normal distributions with the same fixed variance \sigma_t^2, so they have a closed form (Closed form of the KL divergence for normal distributions), which only depends on the distance between their means:

    \text{KL}(q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) || p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t)) = \dfrac{1}{2 \sigma_t^2} \, || \tilde{\mu}_t(x_t, x_0) - \mu_\theta(x_t, t) ||^2 + \text{cst}

Both means were written in the same form in the previous section, with the true noise \epsilon for \tilde{\mu}_t and its prediction \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) for \mu_\theta. Their difference is therefore proportional to the error of the network:

    \text{KL}(q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) || p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t)) = \lambda_t \, || \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) ||^2 + \text{cst} \qquad \text{with} \qquad \lambda_t = \dfrac{\beta_t^2}{2 \, \sigma_t^2 \, \alpha_t \, (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t)}

Maximizing the ELBO is therefore a weighted sum of T regression problems: at each step, predict the noise contained in the noisy sample. Ho et al. (2020) found that ignoring the weights \lambda_t gives better samples in practice, which leads to the remarkably simple loss:

    \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim p(x_0), \, t \sim \mathcal{U}(1, T), \, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)} [|| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \, \epsilon, t) ||^2]

The sum over the T steps has been replaced by an expectation over a random step t, estimated with Monte Carlo as everything else. Thanks to the one-shot formula of the forward process, training never simulates the forward process step by step. Each training iteration consists in:

sampling a data sample x_0 from the training set, a step t uniformly between 1 and T, and a noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I);
computing the noisy sample x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \, \epsilon;
updating the network to reduce the squared error || \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) ||^2 between the true and the predicted noise.

A diffusion model is therefore trained as a denoiser: a single network learns to remove noise from data at all noise levels at once. The simplicity and stability of this training, a plain regression without adversarial game or approximate posterior, is one of the main reasons for the success of diffusion models.


Mass-covering, but not blurry
The training objective is a lower bound of the log-likelihood of the data, and each KL term has the distribution derived from the data as its first argument: like the VAE, a diffusion model is trained in the direction of maximum likelihood, i.e. by minimizing the forward KL divergence between the data and the model (Forward vs. reverse KL). A more general rule of thumb is that objectives defined as expectations over the data are mass-covering (maximum likelihood, VAEs, diffusion models), while objectives defined as expectations over the model’s own samples are mode-seeking (variational inference). With a suitable weighting of the noise levels, the training objective of diffusion models is indeed a bound on the KL divergence between the data and the model (Song et al., 2021a).
Forward vs. reverse KL showed that the forward KL produces “averaged” fits between the modes of the data when the model is not flexible enough, which explains the blurriness of VAEs. Diffusion models escape this fate because their family of distributions is very flexible. Each reverse step only has to be approximately normal, which is accurate for small steps, and the composition of many such steps can represent arbitrarily complex, multimodal distributions. The forward KL only averages between modes when the model cannot represent them; a chain of many small Gaussian steps can.

title: Denoising diffusion models
text:
Sampling

Running the reverse process
Once the network is trained, generating a new sample is a direct application of ancestral sampling (Sampling from simple distributions): sample the last latent variable from the prior, then each latent variable given the next one, down to x_0:

sample pure noise x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I);
for t = T, T-1, \ldots, 1: predict the noise \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) contained in the current sample, and sample the previous step: 
x_{t-1} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \, \left( x_t - \dfrac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}} \, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \right) + \sigma_t \, z \qquad \text{with} \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

return x_0 (no noise is added in the very last step).

Each step removes part of the predicted noise from the current sample, and adds back a smaller amount of fresh noise. The resulting dynamics look very much like Langevin dynamics (Langevin dynamics): a deterministic move in a direction given by the network, plus some noise. The next section shows that this is not a coincidence.
Figure 17.4 shows this reverse process on the two-dimensional mixture of Figure 11.1. For this simple data distribution, the noise predictor that a perfect network would learn can be computed exactly, so the figure shows what an ideal diffusion model does, without any training. The samples start as a standard normal distribution, progressively split into two groups, and end up as samples of the data distribution. At each step, their distribution matches the distribution q(x_t) of the forward process (contours): the reverse process exactly undoes the forward process, one step at a time. The proportions of the two modes are also correct: about 60% of the final samples end up in the lower-left mode, as in the data, whereas the Langevin chains of Figure 11.2 initially split equally between the modes.

SnapshotsAnimation








Figure 17.4: The reverse process on the two-dimensional mixture of Figure 11.1, with the exact optimal noise predictor and T = 1000 steps. Samples (dots) start from a standard normal distribution at t = 1000 and end as samples of the data at t = 0; the contours show the distribution q(x_t) of the forward process at the same step.








The reverse process simulated step by step: starting from pure noise, the samples progressively gather into the two modes of the data distribution.







Faster sampling
The main drawback of diffusion models is their sampling speed: generating a single sample requires T evaluations of the network, typically T = 1000, where a VAE needs a single evaluation of its decoder. Much research has been devoted to reducing this number.
A first improvement is to learn the variances \sigma_t of the reverse steps instead of fixing them: the reverse process can then skip steps, and keeps a good sample quality with only about 50 steps, while also improving the log-likelihood of the model (Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021).
Denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIM) (Song et al., 2022) go further, without any change to the training: they use the same trained network, but a different sampling procedure. At each step, the predicted noise gives an estimate of the clean sample, \hat{x}_0 = (x_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)) / \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}, and the next sample is obtained by noising this estimate again to the level of the next step, reusing the predicted noise instead of drawing a new one:

    x_{t'} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t'}} \, \hat{x}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t'}} \, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \qquad \text{with} \qquad t' < t

Two things change compared to the reverse process above:

The sampling is deterministic: no new noise is added, so a given initial noise x_T always leads to the same sample x_0. The initial noise acts as a latent representation of the generated sample, which can for example be interpolated.
The next step t' does not have to be t - 1: the sampler can skip steps, and only visit a few tens of the T noise levels. With the exact noise predictor of Figure 17.4, 50 DDIM steps already produce samples with the correct modes, proportions and spreads.

Since then, better numerical integration schemes have reduced the number of steps further, and distillation techniques train networks that generate a sample in a few steps, or even a single one.

title: Denoising diffusion models
text:
Diffusion models learn the score

The noise predictor is a score
The network is trained to predict the noise contained in a noisy sample, with a squared error. The best possible prediction for a squared error is the expected value: a perfect network outputs the average noise that could have produced the noisy sample, \epsilon^*(x_t, t) = \mathbb{E}[\epsilon | x_t]. This average turns out to be proportional to the score of the noisy distribution q(x_t) (The score):

    \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t) = - \dfrac{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon | x_t]}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}}







NoteDerivation





The noisy distribution is a mixture of the normal distributions q(x_t | x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \, x_0, \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}) over the data: q(x_t) = \int q(x_t | x_0) \, p(x_0) \, dx_0. Its gradient is therefore:

    \nabla_{x_t} q(x_t) = \int \nabla_{x_t} q(x_t | x_0) \, p(x_0) \, dx_0 = \int q(x_t | x_0) \, \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | x_0) \, p(x_0) \, dx_0

Dividing by q(x_t), and using Bayes’ rule q(x_0 | x_t) = q(x_t | x_0) \, p(x_0) / q(x_t), the score of the mixture is the average of the scores of the components, weighted by their posterior probability:

    \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim q(x_0 | x_t)} [\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | x_0)]

The score of the normal distribution q(x_t | x_0) is - (x_t - \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \, x_0) / (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) = - \epsilon / \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} (The score), where \epsilon is the noise that leads from x_0 to x_t. Averaging over the possible x_0 gives the result. This is known as Tweedie’s formula (Luo, 2022).



A diffusion model therefore learns the score of the data at all noise levels: the network defines a learned score:

    s_\theta(x_t, t) = - \dfrac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}}

Training it with the simple loss is a form of denoising score matching: learning the score of a distribution from its samples only, by learning to denoise them. This answers the question left open at the end of Limits and the bridge to diffusion models: the score of an unknown data distribution can be learned from data.
Equivalently, the network predicts the average clean sample compatible with the noisy one, \mathbb{E}[x_0 | x_t] = (x_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \, \mathbb{E}[\epsilon | x_t]) / \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}. At high noise levels, many very different clean samples are compatible with x_t, and their average is a blurry mixture of all of them. This averaging is not a flaw: it is exactly what is needed to compute the score at this noise level, and the modes of the data are only separated progressively, as the noise decreases.


Sampling is a Langevin dynamics with decreasing noise
Replacing the noise prediction by the learned score in the reverse step gives:

    x_{t-1} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \, \left( x_t + \beta_t \, s_\theta(x_t, t) \right) + \sigma_t \, z

Up to the rescaling factor 1 / \sqrt{\alpha_t}, which is close to one, this is very close to a step of Langevin dynamics (Langevin dynamics) with step size \eta = \beta_t: a move along the score, plus some noise. The difference is that the score changes at each step: it is the score of the data blurred by a decreasing amount of noise. Sampling a diffusion model is therefore an annealed Langevin dynamics, which starts on a very blurred version of the data distribution and progressively sharpens it. This is exactly the idea of the score-based generative models of Song and Ermon (2020), which learn the score at several noise levels and run Langevin dynamics while decreasing the noise: diffusion models and score-based models are two views of the same family of models.
Figure 17.5 shows the score of the noisy distributions on the two-dimensional mixture. This view explains how diffusion models solve the two problems of Langevin dynamics with a learned score raised in Limits and the bridge to diffusion models:

The score is learned everywhere. At high noise levels, the noisy data cover the whole space, so the score is learned in the regions where samples start, and it is a simple field pointing towards the bulk of the data.
The modes are correctly weighted. At high noise levels, the noisy distribution has a single mode, which the samples reach easily. The modes of the data appear progressively as the noise decreases, and each sample commits to one of them while they are still close and connected: the samples are distributed between the modes in proportion to their mass, as in Figure 17.4, instead of being trapped in the nearest mode as the Langevin chains of Figure 11.2.







Figure 17.5: Score of the noisy distribution q(x_t) of the forward process (arrows) on the two-dimensional mixture of Figure 11.1, at decreasing noise levels; contours show the density. At high noise (t = 1000), the score is a simple field pointing towards the origin, defined everywhere; as the noise decreases, it progressively separates the two modes.





Continuous time
The forward process adds a small amount of noise at each of T steps. When the number of steps goes to infinity and each step becomes infinitely small, the sequence of noisy samples becomes a continuous trajectory x(t), with t now a continuous time between 0 and 1. Its evolution is described by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) (Song et al., 2021b):

    dx = - \dfrac{1}{2} \, \beta(t) \, x \, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)} \, dW

An SDE describes how a random trajectory changes during an infinitesimal time dt. The first term, the drift, is a deterministic move: here a slow shrinking towards the origin. The second term is a random kick: dW is a Gaussian increment with zero mean and variance dt (a Brownian motion), scaled by \sqrt{\beta(t)}. Discretizing this equation with a time step dt = 1 gives back the forward step of DDPM: x_t = (1 - \frac{1}{2} \beta_t) \, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t} \, \epsilon \approx \sqrt{1 - \beta_t} \, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t} \, \epsilon. This SDE progressively transforms any data distribution into a standard normal distribution, by spreading the probability mass like heat in a solid: hence the name diffusion.
A classical result of stochastic calculus states that such a process can be run backwards in time, with another SDE whose drift involves the score of the distribution q_t(x) of the noisy samples at time t:

    dx = \left[ - \dfrac{1}{2} \, \beta(t) \, x - \beta(t) \, \nabla_x \log q_t(x) \right] dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)} \, d\bar{W}

where time now runs from t = 1 to t = 0 (dt < 0) and d\bar{W} is a Brownian motion running backwards. Starting from samples of the standard normal distribution at t = 1 and solving this equation backwards produces samples of the data at t = 0. The only unknown quantity is the score, which is exactly what the network learns: replacing it by s_\theta(x, t) and discretizing the reverse SDE with a time step of -1 gives back the reverse step of DDPM of the previous section. The structure of this equation is the one of Langevin dynamics (Langevin dynamics): a move along the score, plus noise.
The same distributions q_t(x) can also be obtained without any noise, by following an ordinary differential equation, the probability flow:

    \dfrac{dx}{dt} = - \dfrac{1}{2} \, \beta(t) \, \left[ x + \nabla_x \log q_t(x) \right]

Each trajectory is now deterministic: a given initial noise always leads to the same sample, but the distribution of the samples at each time is the same as with the reverse SDE. Compared to the reverse SDE, the score term is halved and the noise is removed: the noise of the SDE spreads the samples, which half of the score term compensates on average. DDIM is a discretization of this deterministic flow, which explains why it is deterministic and can take large steps: ordinary differential equations can be solved with efficient numerical methods.
This continuous view unifies the different diffusion models: they differ by the SDE they use (the choice of \beta(t)) and by the numerical method used to solve the reverse SDE or ODE, not by what the network learns. It also connects diffusion models to another family of generative models, which learn a deterministic flow from noise to data directly, without going through a noising process: flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023), presented in a later chapter.

title: Conditional and latent diffusion
text:
Conditional generation
The diffusion models of Denoising diffusion models learn to sample the distribution of their training data. This is not enough for most applications: we do not want an image, but an image of a cat, an image matching a text description, or the most plausible image given some incomplete measurements. In terms of distributions, the data distribution has many modes, for example one for the images of cats and one for the images of dogs, and an unconditional diffusion model sends each initial noise towards one of them, without any control over which one. A conditional model should send all the samples towards the mode we ask for (Figure 18.1).
This chapter presents how diffusion models are conditioned on such information, and how they are made efficient enough to generate high-resolution images, by working in the latent space of an autoencoder.

title: Conditional and latent diffusion
text:
Conditioning the network
A conditional diffusion model learns the distribution p(x_0 | c) of the data given a condition c: a class label, a text description, a low-resolution version of the image… The simplest way is to give the condition as an additional input to the network, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, c, t), and to train it on pairs (x_0, c) with the same loss as before. Everything else is unchanged: the network now learns the score of the noisy conditional distribution, \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | c), and the reverse process generates samples of p(x_0 | c).
In practice, conditioning alone often produces samples that do not match the condition strongly enough: the model also has to represent the variability of the data, and generates plausible but ambiguous samples. Guidance methods modify the sampling process to make the samples more characteristic of their condition.


Classifier guidance
Bayes’ rule relates the conditional and the unconditional noisy distributions through a classifier q(c | x_t), which predicts the condition from a noisy sample:

    q(x_t | c) = \dfrac{q(c | x_t) \, q(x_t)}{q(c)}

Taking the gradient of the logarithm with respect to x_t, the normalization q(c) disappears, and the conditional score is the sum of the unconditional score and of the gradient of the classifier:

    \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | c) = \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t) + \nabla_{x_t} \log q(c | x_t)

Classifier guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021) uses this decomposition with an unconditional diffusion model and a separately trained classifier. The gradient of the classifier, computed by backpropagation through the classifier network, tells in which direction the noisy sample should move to look more like the condition. Multiplying this term by a guidance scale \gamma > 1 strengthens the condition:

    \nabla_{x_t} \log \tilde{q}_\gamma(x_t | c) = \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t) + \gamma \, \nabla_{x_t} \log q(c | x_t)

This is the score of the guided distribution \tilde{q}_\gamma(x_t | c) \propto q(x_t) \, q(c | x_t)^\gamma, which is the conditional distribution for \gamma = 1: the samples are pushed towards the regions where the classifier is the most confident. The classifier has to work on noisy samples at all noise levels, so it must be trained specifically for this purpose.
The same idea applies to the inverse problems of Inverse problems: the condition can be a set of measurements y, and the classifier is replaced by the likelihood p(y | x) of the measurements, which is known when the measurement process is known. An unconditional diffusion model trained on images then becomes a prior for image restoration, without any retraining (Figure 18.2).






Figure 18.2: Reconstruction of an MRI image from partial measurements (bottom right, in the frequency domain): the reverse process of an unconditional diffusion model is guided at each step by the measurements. Source: Song et al. (2022)





Classifier-free guidance
Classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022) obtains the same effect without any classifier. Applying Bayes’ rule the other way around, the gradient of the classifier is the difference between the conditional and the unconditional scores:

    \nabla_{x_t} \log q(c | x_t) = \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | c) - \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t)

Replacing it in the guided score gives:

    \nabla_{x_t} \log \tilde{q}_\gamma(x_t | c) = \gamma \, \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | c) + (1 - \gamma) \, \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t)

The guided score only involves the conditional and the unconditional scores, which can both be learned by the same network: during training, the condition is replaced by a “null” condition for a fraction of the examples (typically 10 to 20%), so that the network learns both \epsilon_\theta(x_t, c, t) and \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing, t). During sampling, the two predictions are combined at each step:

    \tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, c, t) = \gamma \, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, c, t) + (1 - \gamma) \, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing, t)

With \gamma = 0, the model is unconditional; with \gamma = 1, it samples the conditional distribution; with \gamma > 1, it extrapolates beyond the conditional prediction, away from the unconditional one. Most text-to-image models use classifier-free guidance with a scale between 3 and 10.
Figure 18.3 illustrates the effect of the guidance scale on a toy problem with two overlapping classes, where the conditional and unconditional scores can be computed exactly. Without guidance, the samples follow the mixture of the two classes; conditioned on the upper-right class, they follow its distribution, including the region where it overlaps with the other class; with guidance, they are pushed away from the other class, and concentrate on the samples that are the most characteristic of their own.






Figure 18.3: Classifier-free guidance on two overlapping classes (contours), conditioned on the upper-right class. Left: unconditional samples. Middle: conditional samples. Right: guided samples, pushed away from the region shared with the other class. The scores are computed exactly for this toy problem.



Guidance therefore trades diversity for fidelity: the guided samples match their condition better, and are often perceived as being of higher quality, but they are less varied, as they ignore the less typical members of their class. In the terms of Forward vs. reverse KL, the model is trained in the mass-covering direction, and guidance makes its sampling mode-seeking.


Text conditioning
The condition does not have to be a class: it can be any vector, in particular the embedding of a text description (the prompt) computed by a pretrained language model. The prompt embedding is given to every block of the denoising network, usually through attention layers, together with the embedding of the step t (Figure 18.4), and classifier-free guidance strengthens the match between the image and the text.






Figure 18.4: A U-Net conditioned on a text prompt: the embeddings of the time step and of the prompt are given to every block of the network, the prompt through attention layers. Source: https://deepsense.ai/blog/diffusion-models-in-practice-part-1-a-primers/



The best results are obtained with text embeddings that were trained to be aligned with images, such as the ones of CLIP (Radford et al., 2021). CLIP learns a text encoder and an image encoder together, on pairs of images and their captions, by contrastive learning (Figure 18.5): in a batch of pairs, the embeddings of each image and of its own caption are pulled together, while the embeddings of mismatched pairs are pushed apart. Text and images then live in a shared embedding space, where the embedding of a prompt describes what the corresponding images should look like.






Figure 18.5: Contrastive learning in CLIP: the embeddings i_k of the images and t_k of their captions are trained so that matching pairs (diagonal) are similar, and mismatched pairs (off-diagonal) dissimilar. Source: https://deepsense.ai/blog/diffusion-models-in-practice-part-1-a-primers/

title: Conditional and latent diffusion
text:
Latent diffusion models

Diffusion in a latent space
The diffusion models of Denoising diffusion models work directly on the pixels of the images. This is very expensive for high-resolution images: a 512 \times 512 color image has almost 800 000 dimensions, and every step of the reverse process runs a large U-Net on all of them, hundreds of times per generated image. Most of this computation is spent on details that are hardly perceptible, such as the exact value of neighboring pixels, which are highly redundant.
Latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., 2022) separate the two problems. An autoencoder is first trained to compress images into a much smaller latent space, for example 64 \times 64 \times 4 values instead of 512 \times 512 \times 3, and to reconstruct them from it. A diffusion model is then trained in this latent space: the forward process adds noise to the latent representations z = \mathcal{E}(x) of the training images, and the network learns to denoise them (Figure 18.6). To generate an image, the reverse process produces a latent representation from noise, which the decoder \mathcal{D} transforms into an image in a single pass.






Figure 18.6: Latent diffusion: an autoencoder (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{D}) maps images to a latent space (left), where the diffusion process and the denoising U-Net operate (middle). The conditioning information (text, semantic maps, images…) is encoded by \tau_\theta and given to the U-Net through cross-attention layers (right). Source: Rombach et al. (2022)



This division of labor matches the strengths of both models. The autoencoder handles the perceptual compression: it removes the redundancy of the pixels and is responsible for the fine details of the reconstruction. The diffusion model handles the semantic content: it learns the distribution of the latent representations, i.e. what images look like, in a space that is much smaller and therefore much cheaper to process. In the terms of Latent variable models, the autoencoder provides coordinates on the manifold of images, and the diffusion model learns the distribution of the data on this manifold.
The autoencoder is close to the VAEs of Variational autoencoders, with a small weight on the regularization term, so that the latent space is regular without losing information, and with additional losses that make the reconstructions sharp. This is the family of models behind Stable Diffusion, and most current text-to-image and video generators are latent diffusion models conditioned on text, as in Conditional generation.


Back to the VAE
Latent diffusion models solve, in a sense, the problem of VAEs raised in Variational autoencoders. A VAE assumes that the latent representations follow a simple prior, the standard normal distribution, and its decoder must cope with the mismatch between this prior and the actual distribution of the encoded data, which leads to blurry samples. In a latent diffusion model, the latent space is not required to follow a simple distribution: the diffusion model learns the distribution of the latent representations, whatever its shape. The diffusion model is a learned, very expressive prior for the latent space of the autoencoder.
The autoencoder and the diffusion model can even be trained together, the diffusion model playing the role of the prior in the ELBO of the VAE (Vahdat et al., 2021) (Figure 18.7): the regularization term \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) || p(z)) of Variational inference then compares the encoder with the distribution learned by the diffusion model, instead of a fixed normal distribution.






Figure 18.7: A VAE whose prior p(z_0) is a diffusion model in its latent space, trained end-to-end. Source: Vahdat et al. (2021)

title: Conditional and latent diffusion
text:
Modern text-to-image models
The text-to-image generators that appeared from 2022 onwards combine the ingredients of this chapter in different ways. Their details change with each new version, but their main architectural ideas illustrate well how the pieces fit together.

Stable Diffusion
Stable Diffusion is the open-source implementation of latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022): an autoencoder compresses the images, a U-Net conditioned on a CLIP text embedding through cross-attention performs the diffusion in its latent space, and classifier-free guidance strengthens the match with the prompt (Figure 18.6). Its weights are publicly available, which made it the basis of a large ecosystem of fine-tuned models and extensions, conditioned not only on text but also on sketches, depth maps or poses.
GLIDE (Nichol et al., 2022) had shown shortly before that diffusion models conditioned on text, with classifier-free guidance, produce photorealistic images, and that the same model can edit existing images by inpainting: generating new content in a masked region, consistent with the rest of the image, which is the inverse problem of Inverse problems with a text condition.


DALL-E 2
DALL-E 2 (Ramesh et al., 2022) makes explicit use of the shared embedding space of CLIP. The generation is split into two steps (Figure 18.8):

A prior transforms the CLIP embedding of the text into a plausible CLIP embedding of an image. This step is necessary because the embeddings of a caption and of its image are close but not identical: many images match the same caption. The prior is itself a diffusion model, working on embedding vectors instead of images.
A decoder, a diffusion model conditioned on the image embedding, generates the image itself, followed by diffusion models that increase its resolution.

As the decoder inverts the image encoder of CLIP, the approach is also called unCLIP. Sampling several images from the same image embedding produces variations of an image that share its content and style.






Figure 18.8: DALL-E 2 (unCLIP). Top: CLIP learns a shared embedding space for texts and images. Bottom: a prior maps the text embedding to an image embedding, and a diffusion decoder generates the image from it. Source: Ramesh et al. (2022)





Imagen
Imagen (Saharia et al., 2022) works directly in pixel space, with a cascade of diffusion models (Figure 18.9): a first model generates a small 64 \times 64 image from the text, and two super-resolution diffusion models successively increase its resolution to 256 \times 256 and 1024 \times 1024, each conditioned on the text and on the lower-resolution image. Each model of the cascade only has to solve a simpler problem: the first one the global composition of the image, the next ones the details.
Its other main finding concerns the text encoder: instead of a CLIP encoder, Imagen uses a large language model trained on text only (T5), whose weights are frozen. Increasing the size of this text encoder improved the quality of the images and their match with the prompt much more than increasing the size of the diffusion models: understanding the prompt is as important as generating the image.






Figure 18.9: Imagen: a cascade of a text-conditioned image generator and of two super-resolution diffusion models, all conditioned on the embedding of a frozen language model. Source: https://imagen.research.google





Current trends
Two evolutions have marked the most recent generations of models. First, the U-Net is increasingly replaced by transformers operating on patches of the latent representation (Peebles and Xie, 2023), which scale better with the size of the model and of the data, as they did for language. Second, many recent models, including recent versions of Stable Diffusion (Esser et al., 2024), are no longer trained as diffusion models in the strict sense, but with flow matching, which learns a deterministic flow from noise to data: the subject of the next chapters.

title: Conditional and latent diffusion
text:
Summary
Diffusion models gather most of the ideas of this book in a single framework. The following table summarizes the role played by each of them:








Ingredient

In short, a diffusion model:

destroys the data progressively with a fixed noising process, whose noisy samples at any step are obtained in one operation;
learns a single network to undo one step of noise, trained with a simple regression on the noise, which is a lower bound of the log-likelihood of the data and a form of denoising score matching;
generates new samples by running the learned reverse process from pure noise, a noisy Langevin dynamics with decreasing noise, or a deterministic flow for faster sampling;
can be conditioned on classes, texts or measurements, and guided to trade diversity for fidelity;
is usually trained in the latent space of an autoencoder, which makes it efficient enough for high-resolution images.

The continuous-time view of Denoising diffusion models opens the way to another family of generative models, which learn a deterministic flow transporting the noise onto the data, without going through a noising process. Learning such a flow raises a new question: among all the ways of transporting one distribution onto another, which one is the best? This is the subject of optimal transport, presented in the next chapter, before flow matching.

title: Optimal transport
text:
Comparing distributions without overlap
Throughout this book, distributions have been compared with the KL divergence: maximum likelihood minimizes the KL between the data and the model, variational inference the KL between an approximate and a true posterior, and diffusion models a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians. The KL divergence compares the densities of the two distributions at the same points, and is blind to the geometry of the space in which they live. Optimal transport compares distributions in a different way: by the cost of moving one of them onto the other. It provides distances that remain meaningful when the distributions do not overlap, and, more importantly for generative modeling, paths that transform one distribution into another. These paths are what the flow matching models of the next chapter learn.
Let’s consider two uniform distributions on intervals of length 1: p on [0, 1], and q on [d, d + 1], i.e. the same distribution shifted by d (Figure 19.1). How far apart are they?
This is not an artificial situation. The data of interest typically lie on low-dimensional manifolds of a high-dimensional space (Latent variable models), and a model at the beginning of training puts its mass on a different manifold: the two distributions have practically no overlap. Divergences comparing densities point by point then give little or no information about how to improve the model. This was one of the main difficulties of the original generative adversarial networks, whose training implicitly minimizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence.
What we would like is a measure of the effort needed to transform one distribution into the other. Imagine the density of p as a pile of sand, and the density of q as a hole of the same volume: the effort is the amount of sand that has to be moved, multiplied by the distance it travels. Shifting the pile by a distance d requires moving all the sand by d: the effort grows smoothly with the shift, whether the distributions overlap or not. This is the idea of the earth mover’s distance, formalized by optimal transport: in Figure 19.1, the Wasserstein distance W_2, defined in the next sections, is simply equal to the shift d.

title: Optimal transport
text:
As soon as d > 0, part of the mass of p lies where q is zero, and the KL divergence \text{KL}(p || q) is infinite (Kullback-Leibler divergence). It is infinite for a shift of 0.001 and for a shift of 1000: it says that the distributions are different, but not by how much.
The Jensen-Shannon divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence), which compares both distributions to their average, remains finite. It is equal to d \log 2 as long as the two intervals overlap, as only the non-overlapping parts of length d contribute, but it becomes constant, equal to its maximum \log 2, as soon as they are disjoint (d \geq 1). Its gradient with respect to the shift is then zero: if q was a model, nothing would tell it in which direction to move to get closer to p.







Figure 19.1: Two uniform distributions p and q shifted by d (left), and the divergences between them as a function of the shift (right). The KL divergence is infinite for any shift; the Jensen-Shannon divergence saturates at \log 2 when the supports are disjoint; the Wasserstein distance W_2 simply grows with the shift.

title: Optimal transport
text:
Monge’s problem
The question of moving piles of earth at the lowest cost was formulated by the French mathematician Gaspard Monge in 1781, for the construction of fortifications. In modern terms, we look for a transport map T that moves each point x of the source distribution p to a point T(x), in such a way that the transported points follow the target distribution q:

    x \sim p \quad \Rightarrow \quad T(x) \sim q

The distribution of the transported points is called the push-forward of p by T, and is noted T_\# p: the constraint is T_\# p = q. Moving a unit of mass from x to y has a cost c(x, y); in this chapter, we use the squared Euclidean distance c(x, y) = ||x - y||^2. Among all the maps that transform p into q, Monge’s problem looks for the one with the lowest average cost:

    \min_{T \, : \, T_\# p = q} \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p} [||x - T(x)||^2]

For the shifted uniform distributions of Figure 19.1, the best map is the translation T(x) = x + d: every grain of sand moves by d, and the average cost is d^2. Its square root, d, is the distance plotted in the figure.
Transport maps are nothing new in this book: inverse transform sampling (Sampling from simple distributions) and the reparameterization trick (The reparameterization trick) are maps transforming a simple distribution (uniform or normal) into the desired one, and the decoder of a generative model is a learned map from the latent distribution onto the data distribution. What optimal transport adds is the notion of the best map, the one that moves the mass as little as possible.
Monge’s formulation has two important limitations:

An admissible map does not always exist. If p puts all its mass on a single point, and q splits it between two points, no map can transform p into q: a map sends each point to a single destination, and cannot split its mass.
The constraint T_\# p = q is very difficult to handle: the set of maps satisfying it has no simple structure, and Monge’s problem resisted mathematicians for almost two centuries.

Both limitations disappear when the mass leaving a point is allowed to be split between several destinations, which is the relaxation proposed by Kantorovich.

title: Optimal transport
section: Kantorovich’s relaxation and the Wasserstein distance
text:
Kantorovich’s relaxation and the Wasserstein distance

Couplings
In 1942, the mathematician and economist Leonid Kantorovich proposed to replace the transport map by a transport plan, or coupling: a joint distribution \pi(x, y) over pairs of source and target points, which says how much mass is moved from x to y. The mass leaving a point can now be split between several destinations, and the mass arriving at a point can come from several origins. For the plan to transform p into q, the total mass leaving each point x must be its mass under p, and the total mass arriving at each point y its mass under q. In other words, the marginals of the coupling must be the two distributions:

    \int \pi(x, y) \, dy = p(x) \qquad \int \pi(x, y) \, dx = q(y)

In the discrete case, a coupling is simply a matrix whose rows sum to the probabilities of p and whose columns sum to the probabilities of q. A coupling always exists: the independent coupling \pi(x, y) = p(x) \, q(y), which sends the mass of each source point to all the target points, in proportion of their probability, satisfies both constraints. It corresponds to pairing samples of p and q at random. A transport map T is the special case of a coupling where all the mass of x goes to the single point T(x).


The Wasserstein distance
Kantorovich’s problem looks for the coupling with the lowest average cost:

    \min_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \pi} [||x - y||^2] \qquad \text{over the couplings } \pi \text{ of } p \text{ and } q

Contrary to Monge’s problem, this problem always has a solution, the optimal coupling: the constraints on the marginals are linear, and so is the objective, so that it is a (possibly infinite-dimensional) linear program. When an optimal transport map exists, which is the case for example when p has a density, the optimal coupling is concentrated on this map, and both problems give the same answer.
The minimal cost defines the 2-Wasserstein distance between the two distributions:

    W_2(p, q) = \left( \min_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \pi} [||x - y||^2] \right)^{1/2}

Unlike the KL divergence, it is a true distance between distributions: it is symmetric, zero only when the distributions are equal, and satisfies the triangle inequality. As seen in Figure 19.1, it is finite and informative even when the distributions do not overlap: it measures how far the mass has to travel, not how much the densities differ at each point. Other costs define other distances; in particular, the cost ||x - y|| (without the square) defines the 1-Wasserstein distance W_1, also called the earth mover’s distance.


Optimal transport between samples
In machine learning, the distributions are usually only known through samples. For two sets of N samples \{x_i\} and \{y_j\} with equal weights, the optimal coupling has a very simple form: each source sample is sent entirely to a single target sample, so that the coupling is a permutation, i.e. a pairing of the samples. Finding the optimal pairing is the classical assignment problem, which can be solved exactly, for example with the Hungarian algorithm, in a time growing with N^3.
Figure 19.2 compares two couplings between samples of a standard normal distribution and of the two-dimensional mixture of Figure 11.1. With the independent coupling, the samples are paired at random: the segments joining the pairs are long, go in all directions, and cross each other very often. The optimal coupling pairs each sample with a nearby one: the average squared distance is almost three times smaller, the segments point in consistent directions, from the center towards the two modes, and they cross much less often. These short, consistent segments will play an important role for flow matching, which learns to move samples along such paths.






Figure 19.2: Couplings between 40 samples of a standard normal distribution (blue) and 40 samples of the two-dimensional mixture of Figure 11.1 (orange). Left: independent coupling (random pairs). Right: optimal coupling, obtained by solving the assignment problem; its average squared distance is an estimate of W_2(p, q)^2.

title: Optimal transport
text:
Closed forms
In general, optimal transport has no closed form, and must be computed numerically. Two important special cases are exceptions.

One dimension: sorting
On the real line, the optimal transport for the squared cost is monotone: it never makes two grains of sand cross each other. The smallest source samples are sent to the smallest target samples, the largest to the largest: for two sets of N samples, the optimal pairing is obtained by simply sorting both sets, and pairing them in order. For continuous distributions with cumulative distribution functions F_p and F_q, a point is sent to the point of q with the same rank, i.e. the same quantile:

    T(x) = F_q^{-1}(F_p(x))

This should look familiar: when p is the uniform distribution on [0, 1], F_p(u) = u and the optimal map is T(u) = F_q^{-1}(u), which is exactly inverse transform sampling (Sampling from simple distributions). Inverse transform sampling is the optimal way of transporting uniform samples onto a target distribution. The Wasserstein distance is then the average squared difference between the quantiles of the two distributions:

    W_2(p, q)^2 = \int_0^1 (F_p^{-1}(u) - F_q^{-1}(u))^2 \, du



Normal distributions
Between two univariate normal distributions p = \mathcal{N}(\mu_p, \sigma_p) and q = \mathcal{N}(\mu_q, \sigma_q), the optimal map is the affine function that standardizes the source and rescales it to the target:

    T(x) = \mu_q + \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} \, (x - \mu_p)

With p = \mathcal{N}(0, 1), this is the reparameterization trick of The reparameterization trick: transforming standard normal noise into a sample of \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) with \mu + \sigma \, \xi is optimal transport. The Wasserstein distance has a remarkably simple form:

    W_2(p, q)^2 = (\mu_p - \mu_q)^2 + (\sigma_p - \sigma_q)^2

i.e. it is the Euclidean distance between the parameters (\mu, \sigma) of the two distributions. In several dimensions, the first term becomes ||\mu_p - \mu_q||^2, and the second one a more complex function of the covariance matrices.
It is instructive to compare this result with the KL divergence between the same distributions (Closed form of the KL divergence for normal distributions):

    \text{KL}(p || q) = \log \dfrac{\sigma_q}{\sigma_p} + \dfrac{\sigma_p^2 + (\mu_p - \mu_q)^2}{2 \sigma_q^2} - \dfrac{1}{2}

Both depend on the distance between the means, but in different units. The KL divergence measures it relatively to the width \sigma_q of the distributions: two very narrow distributions with slightly different means have almost no overlap, and a very large KL divergence, which becomes infinite when \sigma \rightarrow 0. The Wasserstein distance measures it in the units of the space itself: two narrow distributions at a distance d are at a Wasserstein distance close to d, however narrow they are. The KL divergence is also not symmetric, whereas the Wasserstein distance is.

title: Optimal transport
text:
Interpolating between distributions

Displacement interpolation
Optimal transport does not only measure how far apart two distributions are: it also describes how to go from one to the other. The simplest way to interpolate between two distributions p and q is the mixture (1 - t) \, p + t \, q, with t going from 0 to 1. The mass does not move: it progressively disappears from p and reappears in q, and the intermediate distributions have two separate bumps (Figure 19.3, left).
Optimal transport suggests another interpolation, called displacement interpolation: move each sample x of p along the straight line towards its destination T(x), at constant speed:

    x_t = (1 - t) \, x + t \, T(x)

The distribution p_t of the moving samples slides from p at t = 0 to q at t = 1 (Figure 19.3, right). The intermediate distributions are genuinely “in between” p and q: between two normal distributions, they are normal distributions whose mean and standard deviation are interpolated linearly. They are also equally spaced in the sense of the Wasserstein distance, W_2(p, p_t) = t \, W_2(p, q): the displacement interpolation is the shortest path between p and q in the space of distributions equipped with the Wasserstein distance.






Figure 19.3: Two ways of interpolating between p = \mathcal{N}(-2, 0.5) (top) and q = \mathcal{N}(2, 1) (bottom). Left: the mixture fades p out and q in, without moving any mass. Right: the displacement interpolation of optimal transport moves the mass along straight lines, and the intermediate distributions slide from p to q.





The dynamic view
This suggests a third, dynamic formulation of optimal transport, in terms of motion rather than of maps or couplings. Let’s describe the transformation of p into q by a velocity field v_t(x): at time t, a particle at position x moves with velocity v_t(x), i.e. follows the ordinary differential equation:

    \dfrac{dx}{dt} = v_t(x)

Starting from samples of p at t = 0, the particles should arrive at time t = 1 distributed according to q. Many velocity fields achieve this. Among them, Benamou and Brenier (2000) showed that optimal transport is the one with the minimal average kinetic energy:

    W_2(p, q)^2 = \min_{v} \; \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_t} [||v_t(x)||^2] \, dt

where p_t is the distribution of the particles at time t. The optimal particles move along straight lines at constant speed, from x to T(x), and two particles are never at the same place at the same time: the velocity field is well defined everywhere.
This dynamic view connects optimal transport to the generative models of the previous chapters. The probability flow of diffusion models (Denoising diffusion models) is also an ordinary differential equation dx / dt = v_t(x) transporting noise onto data, but its trajectories are curved, and it needs many integration steps. A generative model that learned the velocity field of optimal transport from noise to data would move its samples along straight lines, which can in principle be integrated in very few steps. Learning such velocity fields is the idea of flow matching, the subject of the next chapter.

title: Optimal transport
section: Entropic regularization and the Sinkhorn algorithm
text:
Entropic regularization and the Sinkhorn algorithm

Blurring the coupling
Computing optimal transport exactly between large sets of samples is expensive: the assignment problem requires a time growing with N^3, and its solution changes abruptly when the samples move, which makes it difficult to use inside a neural network trained by gradient descent. A very effective alternative is to regularize the problem with the entropy of the coupling (Information theory):

    \min_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \pi} [||x - y||^2] - \epsilon \, H(\pi)

where \epsilon > 0 controls the strength of the regularization. Maximizing the entropy pushes the coupling to be as random as possible, while minimizing the cost pushes it to send each point only to its best destination. The two extreme cases are:

\epsilon \rightarrow 0: the entropy term disappears, and we recover the exact optimal coupling;
\epsilon \rightarrow \infty: only the entropy matters, and the coupling becomes the independent coupling p(x) \, q(y), which is the coupling of maximal entropy with the given marginals.

In between, the regularized coupling is a blurred version of the optimal one: each source point sends its mass mostly to its optimal destination, but also a little to the nearby points.


The Sinkhorn algorithm
The entropic regularization has a remarkable consequence: the optimal coupling takes a very simple form. For samples \{x_i\} and \{y_j\}, it is a matrix of the form:

    \pi_{ij} = u_i \, K_{ij} \, v_j \qquad \text{with} \qquad K_{ij} = \exp \left( - \dfrac{||x_i - y_j||^2}{\epsilon} \right)

The matrix K is fixed: it is large for nearby pairs and small for distant ones, and the temperature \epsilon plays the same role as the temperature of the softmax (Softmax classifier for discrete distributions). The only unknowns are the scaling vectors u and v, one coefficient per sample, which must be chosen so that the rows of \pi sum to the weights of p and its columns to the weights of q. The Sinkhorn algorithm finds them by alternately rescaling the rows and the columns:

rescale the rows: choose u so that each row of \pi has the right sum, u_i = p_i / \sum_j K_{ij} \, v_j;
rescale the columns: choose v so that each column of \pi has the right sum, v_j = q_j / \sum_i K_{ij} \, u_i;
repeat until convergence.

Each iteration only involves products between a matrix and a vector, which run very efficiently on GPUs, and every operation is differentiable, so that the regularized transport cost can be used as a loss function and backpropagated through. Popularized by Cuturi (2013), the Sinkhorn algorithm made optimal transport practical for machine learning, where it is used for example to compare sets of samples, to align distributions between domains, or to compute couplings between minibatches of samples.


Schrödinger bridges
Entropic optimal transport also has a dynamic version. In 1931, Erwin Schrödinger asked the following question: if a cloud of particles, moving randomly by diffusion, is observed in a distribution p at a first time and in a distribution q at a later time, what is the most likely way in which the particles moved between the two observations? The answer, called the Schrödinger bridge, is a stochastic process transporting p onto q, and its coupling between the start and end points is the entropic optimal coupling, with a regularization \epsilon proportional to the amount of diffusion.
When q is the data distribution and p a standard normal distribution, a Schrödinger bridge is a diffusion process transforming noise into data, like the reverse process of a diffusion model. Unlike diffusion models, which need a forward process ending exactly in a standard normal distribution, Schrödinger bridges can connect any two distributions, for example two different datasets of images, and can be learned with score-based methods (Bortoli et al., 2023).

title: Optimal transport
text:
Wasserstein GANs
Generative adversarial networks train a generator by pitting it against a discriminator, and their original formulation implicitly minimizes the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the data and the generated samples, whose gradient vanishes when the two distributions do not overlap (Figure 19.1). Wasserstein GANs (Arjovsky et al., 2017) minimize the 1-Wasserstein distance instead. The coupling formulation is impractical in high dimensions, but the 1-Wasserstein distance has an equivalent dual formulation, which only involves functions of a single variable:

    W_1(p, q) = \max_{f \, : \, 1\text{-Lipschitz}} \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p} [f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q} [f(y)]

where the maximum is over all functions f whose slope is at most 1 everywhere. The function f, called the critic, is a neural network trained to give high values to real data and low values to generated samples; the constraint on its slope, enforced for example by penalizing its gradient, prevents it from separating the two sets infinitely sharply. The generator is trained to minimize the resulting estimate of the distance. As the Wasserstein distance decreases smoothly when the generated samples get closer to the data, even without overlap, the generator receives useful gradients throughout training, which made GANs much more stable.

title: Flow matching
text:
Flows
Diffusion models learn to generate data by learning to undo a noising process, one step at a time (Denoising diffusion models). Their continuous-time version showed that they can also be sampled with a deterministic flow, an ordinary differential equation transporting noise onto data, and Optimal transport showed that some flows are better than others: the ones of optimal transport move the mass along straight lines. Flow matching (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022) learns such a flow directly, with a regression as simple as the one of diffusion models, but without any noising process. It has become the training method of many recent large generative models.
A flow is defined by a time-dependent velocity field v_t(x), which gives, at each time t \in [0, 1] and each position x, the velocity of a particle located there. Starting from a sample of the noise distribution, a particle follows the ordinary differential equation (ODE):
\dfrac{dx}{dt} = v_t(x) \qquad \text{with} \qquad x(0) = x_0 \sim p_0
until it reaches its final position x(1) at t = 1. Moving all the samples of p_0 in this way transforms their distribution: at each time t, the particles follow a distribution p_t, which goes from p_0 at t = 0 to some final distribution at t = 1. The goal of a generative model is to find a velocity field whose final distribution is the data distribution p_1. This is the dynamic view of transport of Optimal transport, and the probability flow of diffusion models (Denoising diffusion models) is one such velocity field.
Figure 20.1 illustrates this in one dimension, with time on the horizontal axis. The velocity field is represented by arrows: at each time and position, it tells in which direction and how fast a particle moves. The particles start from the noise distribution on the left, follow the arrows, and progressively gather into the two modes of the data distribution on the right. In between, their distribution p_t progressively deforms from one into the other.
How the distribution p_t evolves under the flow is described by the continuity equation of fluid mechanics, which expresses the conservation of mass: the probability mass is neither created nor destroyed, so the density at a point only changes because mass flows in or out of it. We will not need its exact form here, only the fact that a velocity field determines how the whole distribution moves.
Models that learn a velocity field v_\theta(x, t) with a neural network are called continuous normalizing flows (Chen et al., 2018). They can in principle be trained by maximum likelihood, as the continuity equation allows computing how the log-density of each sample changes along its trajectory. But this requires simulating the ODE for every training sample, and computing derivatives of the network along the whole trajectory: training is very slow, and scales badly to high-dimensional data such as images. Flow matching avoids this simulation entirely: the velocity field is learned by regression on samples of the paths, without ever solving the ODE during training.

title: Flow matching
section: Conditional paths and the marginal velocity
text:
Conditional paths and the marginal velocity

Straight lines between noise and data
Which velocity field transports the noise onto the data? We do not know it, but we can easily build paths from noise to data. Let’s pick a noise sample x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and a data sample x_1 from the training set, independently of each other, and join them by a straight line travelled at constant speed:

    x_t = (1 - t) \, x_0 + t \, x_1

Along this conditional path, the velocity is constant and very simple:

    u_t = \dfrac{d x_t}{dt} = x_1 - x_0

Repeating this for all pairs of noise and data samples defines a distribution p_t of the interpolated points at each time t. It goes from the noise distribution at t = 0 to the data distribution at t = 1, and blends both in between: for each t, p_t is obtained by shrinking the data by a factor t and blurring it with noise of standard deviation 1 - t. We already have a way to generate samples of p_t for any t, by interpolating random pairs. But generating data requires a velocity field: a rule that tells, for a point x at time t, where to go, without knowing in advance which pair it belongs to.


The marginal velocity
Many conditional paths pass through the same point x at time t: lines between different noise and data samples cross each other (Figure 20.2, left). The velocity field that moves the whole distribution p_t along, called the marginal velocity, is the average of the velocities of all the conditional paths passing through x at time t:

    v_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 \, | \, x_t = x]







NoteWhy the average?





Think of the probability mass flowing through a small region around x at time t. Each conditional path passing through this region carries its own share of the mass with velocity x_1 - x_0. The total flux of mass through the region is the sum of the fluxes of all the paths, i.e. the density p_t(x) multiplied by their average velocity. A single velocity field moving the same amount of mass in the same way must therefore have this average velocity at x. Formally, the continuity equation is linear in the product of the density and the velocity, so the marginal densities and fluxes of the conditional paths add up (Lipman et al., 2023).
As the path is a straight line, the conditional velocity can also be written in terms of the end point: x_1 - x_0 = (x_1 - x_t) / (1 - t), so that v_t(x) = (\mathbb{E}[x_1 | x_t = x] - x) / (1 - t): the marginal velocity points towards the average data sample compatible with the current position, which is what the toy figures of this chapter compute exactly.



The marginal velocity transports the noise distribution onto the data distribution, through exactly the same intermediate distributions p_t as the conditional paths. But its trajectories are not the conditional paths. Each conditional path is a straight line, but the marginal velocity averages over many lines going in different directions, so its trajectories are curved (Figure 20.2, right). A particle does not end at a predetermined data sample: it follows the average direction, and commits progressively to one of the modes. Unlike the conditional paths, the trajectories of the marginal flow never meet, as the velocity field defines a single direction at each point and time.

Right: trajectories of the marginal flow, starting from the same noise samples, computed with the exact marginal velocity; they are curved, and end in the data distribution, but not at the data samples of the left panel.

title: Flow matching
text:
The flow matching loss
We would like to train a neural network v_\theta(x, t) to approximate the marginal velocity, for example by minimizing the squared error between the two at all times and positions:

    \mathcal{L}_\text{FM}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), \, x \sim p_t} [|| v_\theta(x, t) - v_t(x) ||^2]

But the marginal velocity v_t(x) is an average over all the data, which we cannot compute. The key result of flow matching is that we do not need it: regressing on the velocity of the conditional paths, which is known, works just as well. The conditional flow matching loss is:

    \mathcal{L}_\text{CFM}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1), \, x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \, x_1 \sim p_1} [|| v_\theta((1 - t) \, x_0 + t \, x_1, t) - (x_1 - x_0) ||^2]

The two losses differ only by a constant that does not depend on \theta, so they have the same gradients and the same minimum (Lipman et al., 2023). The reason is the same as for the noise predictor of diffusion models (Denoising diffusion models): the best prediction of a quantity in the sense of the squared error is its expected value. The network cannot know from which pair (x_0, x_1) the point x_t comes, so the best it can do is to predict the average of x_1 - x_0 over all the pairs compatible with x_t, which is precisely the marginal velocity.






NoteProof





Expanding the squares, both losses contain the term \mathbb{E}[||v_\theta(x_t, t)||^2], which is the same as the points x_t follow p_t in both cases. The terms that do not involve \theta (the squared norms of the targets) are constants. Only the cross terms remain to compare. For the conditional loss, conditioning on x_t:

    \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_1} [v_\theta(x_t, t) \cdot (x_1 - x_0)] = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_t} [v_\theta(x_t, t) \cdot \mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 | x_t]] = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_t} [v_\theta(x_t, t) \cdot v_t(x_t)]

which is the cross term of the marginal loss. The two losses therefore differ by a constant.



Training a flow matching model is therefore as simple as training a diffusion model. Each training iteration consists in:

sampling a data sample x_1 from the training set, a noise sample x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and a time t \in [0, 1];
computing the interpolated point x_t = (1 - t) \, x_0 + t \, x_1;
updating the network to reduce the squared error || v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0) ||^2.

The structure is the same as the training of diffusion models: sample data, noise and a time, mix them, and regress. Only the mixing and the target differ: a straight interpolation instead of the noise schedule \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}, and the direction from the noise to the data instead of the noise itself. No ODE is ever solved during training, which is the main advantage over continuous normalizing flows. As for diffusion models, the distribution of the times t used during training matters in practice: large models sample them more often in the middle of the interval, where the prediction is the most difficult (Esser et al., 2024).

title: Flow matching
text:
Sampling
Once the velocity field is learned, generating a new sample consists in drawing a noise sample x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and integrating the ODE dx / dt = v_\theta(x, t) from t = 0 to t = 1. The simplest numerical method is the Euler method: the time interval is divided into K steps of size h = 1 / K, and at each step the sample moves in a straight line along the current velocity:

    x_{t + h} = x_t + h \, v_\theta(x_t, t)

Each step requires one evaluation of the network, as one step of the reverse process of a diffusion model. The Euler method is exact when the trajectories are straight lines travelled at constant speed: a single step would then be enough. When the trajectories are curved, following the velocity in a straight line overshoots or undershoots the curve, and more steps are needed.
Figure 20.3 shows the effect of the number of steps with the exact velocity field of Figure 20.2. With a single step, all the samples land on the same point, the mean of the data: at t = 0, the noise sample says nothing about which data sample it will become, so the marginal velocity points towards the average data sample, \mathbb{E}[x_1] - x_0, and a single step follows it all the way. With a few more steps, the samples have time to change direction and split between the two modes, but the modes are still too narrow and their proportions wrong. Around 50 steps, the samples follow the data distribution. The more curved the trajectories, the more steps are needed, which is why straightening the trajectories is an important goal (see below). In practice, higher-order integration methods, which evaluate the velocity at several points of each step, reduce the number of steps further.

title: Flow matching
section: Diffusion models are flow matching models
text:
Diffusion models are flow matching models

Gaussian paths
The straight line is not the only possible conditional path. More generally, flow matching can use any Gaussian path of the form:

    x_t = \alpha_t \, x_1 + \sigma_t \, x_0 \qquad \text{with} \qquad x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

where the coefficients \alpha_t and \sigma_t go from \alpha_0 = 0, \sigma_0 = 1 (pure noise) to \alpha_1 = 1, \sigma_1 = 0 (pure data). The straight line of the previous sections corresponds to \alpha_t = t and \sigma_t = 1 - t. The conditional velocity is then \dot{\alpha}_t \, x_1 + \dot{\sigma}_t \, x_0, where the dots denote the derivatives with respect to time, and the flow matching loss is unchanged otherwise.
This form should look familiar: it is exactly the one-shot formula of the forward process of diffusion models (Denoising diffusion models), \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}} \, x_{\text{data}} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}} \, \epsilon, with time running in the opposite direction. Diffusion models use the coefficients \alpha_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}} and \sigma_t = \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}}, which satisfy \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1: the variance of the samples is preserved along the path. In the plane spanned by x_0 and x_1, this path is not a straight line but an arc of circle: the conditional paths of diffusion models are curved, even for a single pair of noise and data samples.


Velocity, noise and score
For Gaussian paths, the three quantities that a network can be trained to predict, the velocity, the noise and the score, are linear functions of each other. The marginal velocity can be written as:

    v_t(x) = \dfrac{\dot{\alpha}_t}{\alpha_t} \, x + \left( \dfrac{\dot{\alpha}_t \, \sigma_t^2}{\alpha_t} - \dot{\sigma}_t \, \sigma_t \right) \nabla_x \log p_t(x)







NoteDerivation





Along a conditional path, x_1 = (x_t - \sigma_t \, x_0) / \alpha_t, so that the conditional velocity can be written as a function of the current point and of the noise:

    \dot{\alpha}_t \, x_1 + \dot{\sigma}_t \, x_0 = \dfrac{\dot{\alpha}_t}{\alpha_t} \, x_t + \left( \dot{\sigma}_t - \dfrac{\dot{\alpha}_t \, \sigma_t}{\alpha_t} \right) x_0

The marginal velocity is its average given x_t = x, which only involves the average noise \mathbb{E}[x_0 | x_t = x]. By Tweedie’s formula (Denoising diffusion models), this average noise is proportional to the score of p_t: \mathbb{E}[x_0 | x_t = x] = - \sigma_t \, \nabla_x \log p_t(x). Replacing it gives the result.



The velocity is a combination of the current position and of the score of the noisy data distribution. A network trained to predict the noise, as in diffusion models, therefore also defines a velocity field, and conversely. In particular, the probability flow ODE of a diffusion model (Denoising diffusion models) is exactly the marginal flow of flow matching with the variance-preserving path: both transport the noise onto the data through the same intermediate distributions.
Diffusion models and flow matching models are thus two members of the same family. They differ by three choices, rather than by their principle:

the path: an arc of circle for diffusion models, a straight line for the simplest flow matching;
the target of the regression: the noise, the score or the velocity, which are equivalent up to time-dependent factors, but weight the errors differently at different times;
the sampler: a stochastic reverse process or a deterministic ODE, which can both be used with either model.



Why straight paths?
If both families are equivalent, why prefer straight paths? With a straight path, the conditional velocity x_1 - x_0 is constant along the path, which gives the network a simple, well-scaled regression target at all times. More importantly, straight conditional paths tend to give straighter marginal trajectories than the curved paths of diffusion models, which can be integrated with fewer steps. In a large-scale comparison of paths and training targets for text-to-image models, straight paths with an appropriate distribution of training times gave the best results (Esser et al., 2024), and they are now used by many large generative models.
But, as Figure 20.2 showed, straight conditional paths do not make the marginal trajectories straight: with random pairs of noise and data, the marginal velocity averages over crossing paths, and its trajectories curve. Straightening the marginal trajectories requires changing how noise and data samples are paired, which brings optimal transport back.

title: Flow matching
text:
Straightening the flow

Optimal transport couplings
The flow matching loss pairs noise and data samples at random, which is the independent coupling of Optimal transport. But the loss remains valid for any coupling: the conditional paths only have to start from noise and end on data. With the optimal coupling, the pairs are close to each other and their paths point in consistent directions, so that the marginal velocity averages over paths that agree, and its trajectories are close to the straight lines of optimal transport. The optimal coupling of the whole dataset cannot be computed, but it can be computed on each minibatch, with the assignment or the Sinkhorn algorithm, for a small additional cost (Tong et al., 2024): the learned trajectories are straighter, and fewer steps are needed to generate a sample.
Figure 20.4 illustrates this in one dimension, where the optimal coupling of a minibatch is obtained by sorting both sets of samples. The conditional paths of random pairs cross, those of sorted pairs do not (top). With random pairs, the trajectories of the marginal flow are curved; with sorted pairs, all the paths passing through a point agree, and the trajectories are the straight lines of optimal transport (bottom). Interestingly, both flows end at the same points: in one dimension, a flow cannot make two particles cross, and the order-preserving map is the optimal transport map (Optimal transport). The marginal flow of random pairs finds the optimal destinations, but along curved paths, which require more integration steps.






Figure 20.4: Flow matching with random and optimal pairs in one dimension, from the noise (left of each panel) to a bimodal data distribution (right). Top: the conditional paths of a minibatch of training pairs; random pairs cross (left), while optimal pairs, obtained by sorting both sets, do not (right). Bottom: the resulting flows, from the same noise samples. With random pairs, the trajectories of the marginal flow are curved (left); with optimal pairs, they are the straight lines of optimal transport (right). Both reach exactly the same end points.





Rectified flows
Rectified flows (Liu et al., 2022) straighten the trajectories without computing any optimal transport. After training a first flow with random pairs, each noise sample is paired with the data sample that this flow generates from it, by integrating the ODE. These new pairs are much more consistent than random pairs: the flow does not make its trajectories cross, so the straight lines between the start and end points of its trajectories cross much less. A second flow, trained on these pairs, has straighter trajectories, and the procedure, called reflow, can be repeated. After a few iterations, the trajectories are almost straight, and samples can be generated with very few steps, sometimes a single one. Rectified flows are at the heart of recent large-scale image generators, such as recent versions of Stable Diffusion (Esser et al., 2024).

title: Flow matching
text:
Summary
Flow matching learns the velocity field of a flow transporting noise onto data, by a simple regression on the velocity of conditional paths between noise and data samples. Compared to the diffusion models of Denoising diffusion models, it changes a few choices rather than the principle:

Both families learn the same kind of object, a time-dependent vector field (the score or the velocity) that transforms a simple distribution into the data distribution through a continuum of intermediate distributions, and both inherit the ideas of the previous chapters: the reparameterization of the noisy samples, denoising as a regression on conditional expectations, the dynamic view of optimal transport. The straight paths of flow matching make the regression target simpler and the sampling faster, which is why most recent large-scale image and video generators are trained with flow matching, often combined with transformers instead of U-Nets (Esser et al., 2024). The conditioning and guidance methods of Conditional and latent diffusion, and the use of a latent space, apply unchanged.
For a detailed, implementation-oriented presentation of flow matching and its many variants, see Lipman et al. (2024).
